MN202611_1x60yzco7xy.t:
Brydon Carse has not played for England since the fifth Ashes Test in January

England have opened the door for Brydon Carse to return to Test cricket for the tour of South Africa by naming the pace bowler in the Lions squad.

Carse could come into the Test squad as cover for Josh Tongue, who will miss the opener to the three-Test series to be at the birth of his second child.

England have named a 15-man group for the series, which begins in Johannesburg on 17 December. Uncapped Nottinghamshire left-arm spinner Liam Patterson-White is called up for the first time, at the expense of Shoaib Bashir.

Carse has not been part of any England squad since being handcuffed - explained as arrested then de-arrested - outside a nightclub in Derby in August.

Although Derbyshire Police have ended their investigation into a potential assault, Carse has been charged by the Cricket Regulator, with a verdict still to come.

Carse has continued to play for Durham and has remained available for England selection since the Derby incident.

However, England have previously explained his absence by a need for Carse to spend time away from the international arena.

Speaking as the Test and Lions squads were announced on Monday, England selector Marcus North said: "The past few months, under investigation, there has been a time where he has stood back, a time of reflection.

"It's obviously been a challenging time for Brydon, it's one that we haven't felt that the demands of playing international cricket and what he was dealing with wasn't necessarily right for Brydon or for us.

"There have been numerous conversations over this period. The conclusion is we feel he is in a place where we feel we can introduce him back into the England environment and we feel the Lions is the right place for him to come."

England squad for three-Test series in South Africa: Joe Root (captain), Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson, Sonny Baker, Jacob Bethell, Harry Brook, Sam Cook, Jordan Cox, Ben Duckett, Emilio Gay, Dan Lawrence, Liam Patterson-White, Ollie Robinson, Jamie Smith, Josh Tongue.

Selector North on Carse's return to England set-up

Tongue is missing England's one-day series in Australia with a toe injury and is due to see a specialist in the UK.

Depending on the status of his injury, he could play in England's only warm-up game ahead of the South Africa Tests before returning home for the birth, leaving the tourists a seamer light.

Carse will be competing with other Lions seamers Henry Crocombe, Olly Stone, Matthew Fisher, Eddie Jack, Matthew Potts and Mitchell Stanley for the chance to cover for Tongue.

And North confirmed England will call up "one or two" players to the senior squad.

"This is where I feel using the Lions tour to our advantage - we have a very strong bowling group in that Lions programme," he said.

"That enables us to have a look at where they are at, under competition and training."

The tour of South Africa will be England's first under new head coach Stephen Fleming.

With the white-ball team currently in Perth preparing for the first one-day against Australia on Friday, Fleming travelled from his home in New Zealand to meet with the rest of the management and select the Test squad.

Jacob Bethell returns to the Test team for the first time since July following a knee injury.

The left-hander's return creates congestion in the top order after Emilio Gay and Jordan Cox both featured in the 3-0 home win over Pakistan, with North confirming England are yet to settle on their top six for the first Test against South Africa.

All-rounder Sam Curran, touted as a potential replacement for former captain Ben Stokes, was not considered because he is getting married. The wedding was planned before Stokes announced his international retirement during the summer.

England Lions red-ball squad for two first-class matches in South Africa: Shoaib Bashir, Brydon Carse, James Coles, Mason Crane, Henry Crocombe, Matthew Fisher, Jack Haynes, George Hill, Eddie Jack, Ben Mayes, Ben McKinney, Ollie Pope, Matthew Potts, James Rew, Thomas Rew, Mitch Stanley, Olly Stone, Asa Tribe.

England Lions 50-over squad: Rehan Ahmed, Brydon Carse, Mason Crane, Adam Finch, Matthew Fisher, Calvin Harrison, Jack Haynes, George Hill, Ben Mayes, Ben McKinney, Ollie Pope, James Rew, Naavya Sharma, Ekansh Singh, Asa Tribe.

Bashir's omission is eye-catching, given the faith England showed in the off-spinner under Stokes and previous Test coach Brendon McCullum.

Given a debut at the age of 20 and after playing only six previous first-class matches, Bashir was fast-tracked as England's number-one spinner, becoming the youngest England bowler to 50 Test wickets in the process.

However, a broken hand and a lack of form meant he was not picked during last winter's 4-1 defeat in Australia, and conditions meant he bowled in only one of England's six home Tests during the past summer.

Bashir was still the only specialist red-ball spinner given a central contract last month, an indication he remained the first choice, though is now effectively dropped from a squad for the first time in his England career. The 23-year-old will instead join Carse in the Lions.

"Our investment hasn't changed," said North of Bashir. "He is still a very young man, he is someone who we still have a very positive outlook for.

"We look at each Test series in isolation, and we feel Liam gives us the best balance and that spinner for this tour. We continue to be incredibly invested in Shoaib over the winter."

Patterson-White, who turned 28 on Sunday, is called up on the back of strong form for Nottinghamshire and after being given an England development contract.

Last season, his 42 wickets were the most by a spinner in Division One of the County Championship, while he can contribute with the bat too, having made three first-class hundreds.

Patterson-White may also have benefitted from new coach Fleming's links to Nottinghamshire, the county he once captained.

"Liam has got some great attributes," said North. "There is a lot of consistency with Liam and his bowling.

"We feel that has really come and matured during the past two seasons at Nottinghamshire. He has the ability to hold an end, but also get into the game at the back end.

"We're really excited to see Liam in that Test environment. It's recognition of his development over the past year or so."

The Test squad will arrive in South Africa in different groups, with some joining the Lions in late November and others after returning to the UK following their part in the three one-dayers in Australia.

From the Test players who are also involved in the T20 series in Australia, white-ball captain Harry Brook, Bethell and Cox will miss the fifth and final match of the series in order to travel to South Africa.

For Brook, it will be the first England game he has missed since the T20 tour of Ireland last September. In his absence, all-rounder Will Jacks will captain England for the first time.

Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson Becker wants to stay at the club beyond the end of the season, when his current contract expires.

The 34-year-old joined from Roma for £66.8m in 2018 and has made 347 appearances for the Reds.

"Yes [I want to stay], in my mind. I'm focused on playing every game but in my mind I'm happy to stay," said Alisson.

"That depends on a lot of aspects and different situations. But my will is to stay - I'm happy here and my family is happy here.

"I'm still hungry for titles and to delivering good performances. I still want to play at the top level for as long as I can, so that's my thinking."

Last week, Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola said he did not know if this would be Alisson's last season at the club but hoped the goalkeeper could "continue for more time".

Asked if he has had conversations over a new deal, Alisson said: "No, but my agent is talking with the club."

The Brazil keeper did consider a move to Juventus earlier this year but ultimately chose to stay at Anfield.

After a difficult week - with Liverpool losing to Arsenal and then Fenerbahce - Alisson made a number of crucial saves in Sunday's win at Crystal Palace.

The goalkeeper says Liverpool now need to find consistency in order to challenge for silverware.

"Our reality is that we're not doing as well as we can. It doesn't mean that we are not doing well - we are doing well in so many games - but the consistency is not there yet," he said.

"We have a top manager, top players. We are capable of great things but as a team we need to get to a point where we feel: 'We are OK now. We have the confidence. We have everything that's needed to win.'

"We are building that. I hope we get there really quick but it takes time.

"We have to be patient but as players, in our mind, we don't have time to waste."

Of course, both command hefty wages, but this is a young Liverpool side trying to find their way under Iraola - and the head coach will be aware of the importance of two experienced players who have been with the club for such a long time.

Perhaps a one-year extension can be offered to Alisson which could allow Brughmans to learn from the Brazilian but, at 34, he may be looking for the security of something longer term.

Chris Devane says his players will be banned from the "distraction" of the FA Cup second round draw

The manager of seventh-tier Berkhamsted says his players have been banned from the "distraction" of the FA Cup second round draw.

The Hertfordshire club travel to fellow Southern League Premier Division South side Plymouth Parkway in the final tie of the first round on Monday, with the draw to be made ahead of the 19:30 kick-off.

The tie will be broadcast to an international television audience, and, like their hosts, Berkhamsted have never previously reached this stage of the competition.

"I've told the players they're not allowed anywhere near it [the draw]. Someone could tell me if they want who we get. I'm not really bothered about it," said Comrades boss Chris Devane.

Plymouth Parkway players dream of glamorous FA Cup tie

"It's important the players are focused on what they're there to do and that's win a football game. There's no point losing focus about who you may play if you do win, if you end up jeopardising the opportunity to win by doing so.

"The players will be nowhere near it. I've told them all, let me deal with all the press, let me deal with the TV interviews. You guys have got a job to do. Let me worry about sweeping the floor, so to speak, so that's what the plan is."

Berkhamsted, formed in 2009 after Berkhamsted Town folded, have beaten Bishop's Stortford, Hendon, Redditch United and Southend United to reach this stage - winning £20,625 from the FA's prize fund in the process.

The winners of Monday's tie will take £47,750, with £15,800 going to the losers. Both clubs will also pocket £50,000 for the tie being selected for broadcast.

The Comrades travelled down to Devon on Sunday, with their part-time players due to return home on Tuesday - and many needing to take unpaid leave from work.

Speaking to BBC Three Counties Radio, Devane said: "I'm really intrigued to see how much will a proper day of rest, prep and pre-match meal actually helps them [my players]."

The birds (pictured previously) have returned to the park after being cared for by the USPCA

Resident birds have returned to Broughshane Waterfowl Park after an oil spill which caused the death of 13 of the flock.

The popular attraction in County Antrim was forced to close after a nearby home heating oil tank was vandalised , causing the oil spill into the pond.

In a post on social media, The Waterfowl Pond confirmed that work is still underway to address the oil contamination and that a number of pens remain out of bounds.

More than 20 birds were transported to the USPCA's headquarters for urgent specialist care following the incident.

The park, which was home to 120 birds, has since reopened.

Broughshane Environment Wildfowl and Wildlife Trust's chairman, Gary Hayward, said about 10-12 birds have returned including two black swans and Nenes.

Hayward said they are back safely in their pens and they are lucky to be healthy.

The birds returned to the park on Monday morning

The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) was first alerted to the incident on Thursday 22 October and have been involved in removing the oil waste.

The agency said the substance involved had been identified as home heating oil or kerosene.

Police said about 44 gallons (200 litres) of oil had leaked from the tank which had been damaged at a business premise in the Main Street area of Broughshane.

Hayward said that there is very little evidence of the oil left as the NIEA have removed the majority of it.

"They have made problems a lot less than they could have been," he told BBC News NI.

He said there is still some oil around the edges, and once the oil leaves the pens the birds will be moved back into them.

Gary Hayward said the USPCA were a "great help" at looking after the birds

The USPCA has also been a key part of the rescue operation.

They said that all of the birds, including geese, ducks and swans, needed bathed and treated due to the level of contamination they suffered.

Unfortunately some had already ingested too much and died as a result.

Several birds were injured after the incident

The Waterfowl Pond offered thanks to the USPCA for looking after the birds.

"We are truly grateful for everything you have done."

It also paid tribute to the support received from the public.

"It's another positive step forward for our park, and we couldn't have got here without you."

Police have said that enquiries into the incident are ongoing and have appealed to anyone with information to come forward.

The Booker Prize 2026 judges are Rebecca Liu, Jarvis Cocker, Dame Mary Beard, Raymond Antrobus and Patricia Lockwood

Past Booker Prize winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart are among the contenders to scoop the prestigious literary award this year, after a shortlist selection process that the judges described as "a tussle".

Jamaican writer James is nominated this year for his latest novel The Disappearers; while Scottish author Stuart is shortlisted for John of John.

This year's other contenders are award-winning US novelist Elizabeth Strout, and British authors M John Harrison, Luke Kennard and Rebecca Perry.

But seven books that appeared on the longlist in July were jettisoned, and Dame Mary Beard, who chaired the judging panel, said agreeing on the final six "has been, to put it mildly, hard work".

The winner will receive £50,000 and will be announced in London on Monday evening. The ceremony will be broadcast live on a special edition of BBC Radio 4's Front Row.

Scroll down to find out more about this year's nominees.

James previously won the Booker Prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings, while Stuart won in 2020 for Shuggie Bain.

Praising this year's entries when announcing the shortlist in September, Dame Mary added: "English language fiction now is full of talent – talent old and talent new.

"It's full of wit, seriousness, pleasure, challenge, discomfort and real brilliance, and I think we should be rewarding our novelists a lot more than we do."

The other judges included former Booker Prize-shortlisted US novelist Patricia Lockwood, who said she discovered she was "bossier than I believed myself to be" when making the case for or against particular books in the judges' meetings.

"I was sort of standing up a lot and tossing books across the room and being really active. I was like, 'Wow, yeah, I didn't know I had it in me'."

Another judge, poet Raymond Antrobus, told reporters: "All of us individually had a different idea for a shortlist and then it was a tussle."

Lockwood jokingly added: "A tussle, yeah. We wrestled like pigs in the mud!"

Antrobus said the final choices are connected because they are books that "as well as having heart, also took risk".

"These books, we truly believe, cannot be replicated by artificial intelligence. These are very human books for the way they talk about and navigate a lived experience."

The judging line-up was completed by journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu and Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, who said being on the selection panel was "a bit like being in a band".

He said: "The way a band makes an appealing noise is by everybody combining, in a way, and if you don't like that then you have to go solo.

"You get something that you couldn't get [alone] and no-one's in control of it and you make a good noise together. So I hope that's what this shortlist is, a nice noise."

Cocker read some of the entries while on tour, and said he joined one judges' meeting online while wearing a dressing gown in a hotel room in Australia at 02:00 local time.

"When you're on tour, it's quite dull when you're travelling so it was quite good to have something to read," he said.

"I became known for being in those meetings wearing a towelling robe."

The End of Everything by M John Harrison

An unexplained catastrophe, and the arrival of mysterious alien beings, have turned British society upside down - and a man and his elderly aunt muddle through on the Kent coast. It's the author's first Booker nomination, and he'd be the oldest ever winner at 81.

The judges said: "The End of Everything can be read as a thriller, a mystery, a satire, a dystopia, a road novel, a work of realism. The landscape may be bleak, the catastrophe may be immersive, yet there still were moments we found ourselves laughing aloud."

This epic, visceral story revolves around a violent attack on eight gay men who had gathered to rehearse a queer play in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1988, and its aftermath. The New York Times called it "a masterpiece, the novel of the decade and possibly of the century thus far".

The judges said: "A Jamaican epic from one of the most impactful Caribbean novelists today; readers will love the shifting register of the dialogue and poetic phrasings, often pierced through with sharp, double-edged humour."

An out-of work actor gets a new role - being locked in a black bag during psychology lectures for an entire term as a professor's experiment. The story unfolds into a humorous and poignant satire that makes sharp observations about the state of modern masculinity and creative life.

The judges said: "In a wonderfully quirky campus novel, Kennard combines an absurd experiment with a moving story about human frailty, passion, confusion and identity. There's something for everyone here."

A modern-day museum curator is commissioned to recreate a past scene in a historic palace, and becomes immersed in the world of the young, reluctant king whose life she uncovers. It is the debut novel by Perry, who is also a poet and a former competitive trampolinist.

The judges said: "An affecting and lush jewel of a novel that moves between our present-day world to a medieval court and unsettles the idea that there's ever one universal historical truth."

The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout

Strout, a former Pulitzer Prize winner and double Booker nominee, tells the story of a high school history teacher in his 50s who feels adrift in modern America. When a secret emerges, he must face big questions about his relationships and life choices.

The judges said: "A novel that engages with the deeply divisive politics of present-day America, without itself becoming divisive. This is the kind of book we need now: a calm antidote to contemporary events."

The third novel by Stuart is about a fashion student who is drawn back to his home in a small, religious community in the Outer Hebrides in the mid-1990s. He and his father both nurse secrets. And both are called John.

The judges said: "A rich and moving novel about a father and son who live on a remote Scottish island in the 1990s, where small-town secrets and buried shame reverberate to surprising, devastating and even joyous effect."

Longlisted books that did not make the final cut included Emma Cline's Switzy, which had been seen by some as a frontrunner for the prize.

"Believe me, this is a nailed-on Booker winner," critic Giles Coren wrote in the Times , external this weekend.

"If this one doesn't win, I'll eat Mary Beard."

Dame Mary responded on Tuesday: "I know Giles Coren said he wants to eat me if Switzy isn't on the shortlist.

"Well, I'm going to get the cooker prepared and ask him how he wants me done."

Shygirl is known for big dance bangers, but her latest album has a more stripped-back sound

Hard-hitting beats, club anthems and unapologetically sexy lyrics are what Shygirl is known for.

But the singer and DJ - real name Blane Muise - has introduced a different sound for her second album, Swallow!, which dropped on Friday.

"I've learned over the 10 years I've been making music to have this confidence and to not be afraid of failure," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"The big part of starting this record was wanting to have natural instrumentation and not feel like that was barred from me."

Shygirl puts the change down to a desire for a more "authentic" sound - a growing trend among British electronic artists who've been bringing a rockier influence to their music.

Asked why she took this musical direction, the 33-year-old says it was down to "the nostalgia of the indie sound".

"I felt the familiarity of that feeling, embracing the teenager within and the angst that I had and all the sounds that coloured that environment," she says.

Long-time producers Karma Kid and Casey MQ were "surprised" when Shygirl told them about her desire to work in more indie sounds, but she says the pair trusted her with the new direction.

Fans have been patiently waiting for something other than singles since her debut album Nymph was released in 2022.

The question now is whether they'll relate to this more rose-tinted version of Shygirl.

"It's not like I changed overnight," she insists. "In fact, it was because I was the girl I was in all the other songs that I became who I am now."

The album's artwork shows a chick hatching from an egg, symbolising rebirth

There are clear signs that Shygirl is entering a new chapter.

She cleared her Instagram feed before beginning the album rollout, and the artwork shows a bird hatching from an egg, symbolising rebirth.

But she points out the journey is an "evolution" rather than reinvention.

"I think it's less about moving away from me, but I would hate to repeat myself," she says.

"I would only wish to pick up the same tool if I felt like I had grown somewhat or had a renewed expertise for it."

That growth can be heard in tracks like Live the Life You Like - one of Shygirl's favourites on the album.

It features a gritty bassline and a manipulated riff that echoes a klaxon, which she describes as giving off "punk energy".

Leaning into that side of her sound has only made her more excited to take the record on a tour, starting with Europe in March.

"I've got a band now," she reveals with a grin. "I work with a drummer and a multi-instrumentalist and sometimes a bassist.

"It's just so fun to share the stage and be so inspired. We've rehearsed, but there's still so many moments for spontaneity and for us to look at each other and vibe."

Shygirl's the latest artist known for electronic music who's embraced a more organic sound.

Her close friend Charli XCX featured a rockier, guitar-driven style on her latest album Music, Fashion, Film.

One of the standout tracks on that album for Shygirl is SS26, because "her voice is so natural and exposed".

"You forget other people don't know that voice and they need to get to know that starting point to be able to appreciate everything else."

Shygirl believes that same stripped-back approach is shaping much of the current wave of British dance music, including her latest album.

"There's so many of us now, especially coming from the Brit pack, that are doing the same thing," she says.

Shygirl's friend Charli XCX introduced drums and guitars for her latest album

Artists like PinkPantheress and Fred Again have also spoken about bringing indie influences into electronic music, something Shygirl says is "a reflection of what is going on in the world".

"I think there is a natural desire to have a sense of truth or something grounding," she says.

"And what is more grounding or more truthful than knowing exactly where a sound comes from."

So with artists borrowing more and more from across the musical spectrum, does genre still matter?

For Shygirl, it's less about what box listeners put her music in and more about whether it connects with them.

"Regardless if they like it or they hate it, I want someone to feel something. To be apathetic to my music would be the biggest insult to me."

Jamal Musiala has won 46 caps for Germany

Bayern Munich forward Jamal Musiala may never "regain the performance level he once had", says honorary president Uli Hoeness.

The 23-year-old Germany international collapsed twice in four days during pre-season and it was later revealed he had a treatable "neurological dysfunction".

Musiala has scored two goals in four games for Bayern in all competitions this season.

"We are facing a dilemma in this case, as he is suffering from an illness that cannot simply be cured, but it can be controlled to a certain extent with the use of medication," Hoeness told Bavarian network BR24.

Hoeness said Bayern would support Musiala, who is under contract until 2030.

Former Bayern and Germany captain Lothar Matthaus said Hoeness is trying to motivate Musiala.

"He's needling him a little. It's not just about wrapping him in cotton wool. He also has to battle against adversity sometimes," Matthaus told Sky90.

"Uli was looking to create that adversity with this statement.

"It's fine for him to say something like that, because we can't just put a positive spin on things and somehow wait for him to come back.

"If I were in Jamal Musiala's position, that would be motivation enough to show Uli I'm back."

Musiala joined Bayern in 2019 after coming through Chelsea's academy.

He has scored 71 goals and provided 38 assists in 235 matches for Bayern since breaking into the team as a 17-year-old.

One of the youngest Germany players in history, Musiala shared the Golden Boot as the joint leading scorer at Euro 2024.

He has not played for Bayern since suffering a hamstring injury in September, but recently returned to training.

The embankment collapsed a day after heavy rain flooded tens of thousands of tents across Gaza

Three children and one woman were killed when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents in central Gaza following heavy rain, the Hamas-run health ministry says.

Five injured people were also reportedly rescued after the incident on Sunday night at a camp for displaced families south of Deir al-Balah.

Videos showed men using phone torches to search for survivors beneath boulders, sand and collapsed tents.

The Civil Defence service, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry, said the "humanitarian tragedy" should prompt urgent action by international organisations to provide safe shelters for displaced people and move tents away from sandy areas, slopes and locations at risk of collapse.

Torrential rain on Saturday reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents across Gaza, leaving many Palestinians without a dry place to sleep.

The Civil Defence said water levels reached up to 1.5m (4.9ft) in some places and that its first responders were able to respond to only 10% of the 2,100 distress calls they received.

"Protecting the lives of displaced people is an urgent humanitarian responsibility. Their tents must not become death traps beneath sand and rainwater," it warned.

Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza

Funding shortages force World Food Programme to cut Gaza aid

Eight children among 21 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses, rescuers say

The Civil Defence initially reported on Sunday that three children and two women were killed when the sand embankment collapsed. But the health ministry said on Monday morning that only one woman was among the dead.

She was identified as Tahrir Nabhan, while the children were named as Mariam Nabhan and her brother Salah, and Habiba al-Zein.

Mustafa al-Masri told the BBC that he and other rescuers had used their bare hands to dig the victims and survivors out of the sand and rubble.

"It was extremely difficult. This mound was huge and wide. It collapsed onto the tent, and we didn't know what to do," he said.

"When we got here, we, along with the young men from the camp, pulled them out with our own hands. We pulled out the children and the woman."

"Their father arrived shouting, 'My children, my children, my children, my children.' We pulled his children out, put them in the ambulance, and took them to the hospital."

Masri added that he had been displaced from the northern town of Beit Hanoun but had stayed in central Gaza because there was "nowhere for me to return to".

"We went out looking around, searching through the open areas and hills, but I couldn't find any place other than this area that felt suitable for me."

The rescue operation was made more difficult by the lack of heavy machinery

The International Organization for Migration's regional crisis co-ordinator, Karl Baker, told the BBC from Gaza that the territory's 2.1 million population was confined to only 30% of its total area and that many people were "unfortunately living in areas which would not be normal if we were not in this time of conflict".

He said the UN agency and its partners were trying to make sure there were enough tents and tarpaulins, as well as improved drainage in camps, to help them get through the winter.

However, he warned that aid currently getting into Gaza was not sufficient to meet the demands of the population, describing it as "the very smallest of Band-Aids [plasters]".

"We need more support, in-kind donations. We need funding in order to help the communities to help themselves," he said. "We need a lot more to happen."

UN agencies have called on Israeli authorities to allow in the specialist equipment and materials required to improve living conditions for displaced families.

Cogat, the Israeli military body tasked with co-ordinating deliveries, said on Sunday that more than 91,000 tents, 12 vacuum trucks for waste removal, and fuel and engine oil for pumping facilities have been delivered since the start of the "Gaza Winterization Plan".

But it added that Israel would not permit the entry of equipment that could be used for military purposes by Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups.

An estimated 80% of all structures in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas, according to the UN.

More than 1.9 million people have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, it says.

The UN has warned that the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire despite the ceasefire agreed in October 2025, as Israeli air strikes and other attacks continue to hit populated areas, causing casualties and property damage and driving further displacement.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,640 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Ramla Ali was the first boxer from Somalia to compete at an Olympics

Ramla Ali secured her first world title at the age of 36 after defeating Mikiah Kreps in a split-decision victory in Arlington, Texas.

The win is a crowning moment for the Briton, who fled a war-torn Somalia as a child before going on to become an Olympian, activist, author and now the WBO and IBF super-bantamweight champion.

With her biopic about her remarkable life just released, Ali fulfilled a dream long in the making and that seemed far away when she was swept aside by Yamileth Mercado in her first attempt two years ago.

An emotional Ali fell to her knees in tears as she was confirmed the winner with scorecards that read 97-92, 96-93 and 98-91 in her favour, dedicating the victory to her late father.

"When we were in the changing room, my coach said, because my dad passed away in May, 'Do this for him'," Ali said.

"That's where those emotions came out at the end, because I did it for my dad."

"I can't put into words what this means to me and what this means to all of Somalia," she added.

"I've hopefully inspired so many young girls and boys out there to dream big and that's all I've ever wanted to do."

As Ali wept, there was devastation for Kreps who was convinced she had done enough to win the contest.

The previously undefeated American suffered a knockdown in the third round, walking onto a flush left hook from Ali.

Kreps was unhappy with the knockdown call but replays showed the heavy shot caused the 30-year-old's glove to touch the canvas as she tried to steady herself.

With a 10-8 round in the bag, Ali was unable to build on the moment, having to stand firm as Kreps came storming back and applying constant pressure.

Kreps outlanded Ali with 115 punches to 78 and secured 91 power shots to Ali's 70 and one judge certainly was convinced of her as a clear winner with a wide 98-91 scorecard.

With the fight threatening to slip away from her in the second half, Ali said every round was a mental battle to rise from her stool.

"I remember going to the corner every round and I remember saying 'I'm so tired, I can't do this'. All my coach responded was 'think about your dad, do this for your dad'. I think that really pushed me. I really boxed out of my skin, I was so knackered. I did it for him," Ali said.

"Every time I went to the corner, I kept saying, 'I'm so tired. I'm so tired,' because your work rate was just next level."

Ali speaking in 2022 as her and Crystal Garcia Nova became the first women to box as professionals in Saudi Arabia

With two world titles secured, Ali could set her sights on an intriguing unification bout with Skye Nicolson after the Australia kept hold of her WBC belt on the undercard.

Nicolson is also signed to Jake Paul's Most Valuable Promotions and beat Japan's Miyo Yoshida by unanimous decision.

But Ali will for now celebrate her victory as she delivered yet another high point in an incredible life that might have seen as impossible when her family escaped Somalia when she was just a baby.

Ali settled in London as a refugee and was the first Somali boxer to represent the nation as an Olympian at Tokyo 2020 before becoming the first Muslim woman to win an English title as an amateur.

Since turning pro in late 2020, Ali has been proclaiming her goal to become world champion but saw her credentials in that department derailed in 2023 when she was knocked out in her ninth fight.

As a model often on magazine covers, as well as a dedicated activist for young women running her own non-for-profit organisation Sisters club, many questioned why, and if, Ali should continue boxing.

Those doubters grew louder with the 2023 world title disappointment, but Ali was not to be denied.

Caroline Dubois was in Texas to watch Alycia Baumgardner move up to her weight class

In the main event, Alycia Baumgardner had her post-fight victory speech interrupted by Caroline Dubois.

Baumgardner, 32, outclassed Elif Nur Turhan to become a two-weight world champion by claiming the IBF lightweight belt.

The victory sets Baumgardner on a collision course with British WBO and WBC champion Dubois, who fights WBA belt holder Stephanie Han in February.

After Baumgardner said she wanted to be undisputed at lightweight, Dubois asked her 'are we going to fight' from ringside.

The back-and-forth continued with 25-year-old Dubois repeatedly urging Baumgardner to commit to their contest, while the American insisted she needed to beat Han first.

Dubois is unbeaten in 15 fights, but a victory over Baumgardner - an undisputed champion at super-featherweight and unbeaten since 2018 - would be a potentially career-defining win.

Ikibazo cy'umubano wihariye wa Jensen Huang, umuyobozi mukuru wa Nvidia, cyarenze kure kuba inkuru y'urushako no guca inyuma uwo bashakanye, gihinduka ikibazo kivugwaho cyane mu rwego rw'umutekano wa Amerika.

Ibi biterwa n'uko Nvidia ari imwe muri sosiyete zikomeye cyane ku isi mu gukora ibikoresho bigezweho (chips) bikoreshwa mu bwenge buhangano(AI), mu gihe Amerika n'Ubushinwa biri mu marushanwa akomeye yo kuyobora iri koranabuhanga.

Abayobozi bamwe muri Amerika bavuga ko Huang yagiranye umubano n'umugore bakekaga ko afite aho ahuriye n'ubutasi bw'u Bushinwa.

Ibyo byatumye bamwe mu badepite n'abasenateri batangira kwibaza niba uwo mubano utarashyize mu kaga amabanga y'ikoranabuhanga rya Nvidia cyangwa inyungu z'umutekano wa Amerika.

Kuva mu 2022, Amerika yashyizeho amategeko abuza kohereza mu Bushinwa chips zigezweho n'ubundi buryo bw'ikoranabuhanga bwo mu rwego rwo hejuru. Washington ivuga ko ibyo ari ngombwa kugira ngo igihugu gikomeze kugira akarusho mu marushanwa ya AI kandi kirinde umutekano wacyo.

Ibyo ariko byatumye Nvidia itakaza igice kinini cy'isoko ry'Ubushinwa, n'ubwo ari rimwe mu masoko afite inyungu nyinshi ku isi.

N'ubwo Huang akunze gusaba ko Amerika n'u Bushinwa byakomeza kuganira ku iterambere rya AI no gukorana, ubutegetsi bwa Perezida Donald Trump bwakomeje gufata iri rushanwa nk'ikibazo gikomeye cy'umutekano w'igihugu.

Huang na we yagiye agaragaza ko ashyigikiye inyungu za Amerika ndetse no kurinda umutekano wayo.

Mu itangazo yasohoye, inama y'ubutegetsi ya Nvidia yavuze ko nta kimenyetso na kimwe ifite cyerekana ko amabanga ya sosiyete cyangwa umutekano wa Amerika byaba byarahungabanye.

Huang na we yavuze ko akomeje kwiyemeza gushyigikira no kurinda umutekano wa Amerika.

Minisitiri w'ububanyi n'amahanga wa Amerika, Marco Rubio, yanze kugira ibyo atangaza kuri iki kibazo ubwo yavuganaga n'abanyamakuru mbere yo kwerekeza i Paris mu nama ya G7.

Yagize ati: "Ntabwo nshobora kugira icyo mbivugaho. Ntabwo navuga kuri iki kibazo kubera imiterere yacyo. Kandi sinashobora no kugira icyo mvuga ku bibazo biri imbere muri Nvidia kuko nta makuru mbifiteho."

Icyakora amakuru atandukanye avuga ko Rubio yagize uruhare mu gutegura inyandiko yaburiye ubutegetsi bwa Trump ku mubano uvugwa hagati ya Huang n'umugore w'Umushinwakazi mu mwaka ushize.

Perezida Donald Trump na we yavuze ko kuva amakuru y'iperereza yatangira kujya hanze atongeye kuvugana na Huang.

Yagize ati: "Icyo nzi ni uko ari umuntu mwiza, ariko nyine nta wamenya. Gusa, yakoze akazi kadasanzwe gafitiye igihugu cyacu akamaro."

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Umuvugizi wa minisiteri y'ububanyi n'amahanga, Guo Jiakun, yavuze ko ibirego bivuga ko uwo mugore yaba ari intasi y'u Bushinwa nta shingiro bifite.

Yagize ati: "Twamaze gusubiza kuri ibi birego. Amakuru avuga ku butasi bw'Ubushinwa nta shingiro afite, ni ibitekerezo gusa bigamije guharabika no kwangisha abantu u Bushinwa."

Iki kibazo cyanatumye hibazwa urugero rw'Ubushinwa cyangwa ibindi bihugu bishobora kugerageza kubona amakuru y'ibanga binyuze mu nganda z'ikoranabuhanga.

Umuyobozi mukuru wa Logitech, Hanneke Faber, yabwiye BBC ko buri gihugu na buri kigo gihora gishaka kugira akarusho ku bandi.

Yavuze ko Logitech ishyize imbaraga nyinshi mu kurinda amakuru no kwemeza ko ibanga ry'ibicuruzwa n'imishinga y'iterambere byayo bidashyirwa mu kaga.

"Mu gihe cya AI, umutekano w'amakuru, umutekano wo kuri internet n'ubwirinzi bw'ikoranabuhanga bifite akamaro kurusha ikindi gihe cyose. Turabishoramo imbaraga n'umutungo mwinshi kurusha uko byahoze mbere hose."

N'ubwo kugeza ubu nta kimenyetso gifatika kiragaragazwa cyerekana ko amabanga ya Nvidia cyangwa umutekano wa Amerika byigeze byangizwa n'uyu mubano, iki kibazo cyongeye kugaragaza uburyo intambara y'ikoranabuhanga hagati ya Amerika n'Ubushinwa irimo gutuma n'ibibazo by'ubuzima bwite bw'abayobozi b'amasosiyete bikurikiranwa nk'ibishobora kugira ingaruka ku mutekano w'ibihugu.

Yaba umugore wa Jensen Huang basezeranye mu mategeko cyangwa se uwo bagiranye urukundo rw'ibanga, bose ntawe uragira icyo atangaza ku birimo kuvugwa kuri uyu mugabo.

KIGALI – When Shemsa Umulisa’s father walked into her bedroom one day, he was surprised by what he found. The room was crowded with skincare products, so many that he jokingly wondered whether his daughter had turned it into a beauty shop.

Umulisa, then a secondary school student, had an explanation for every product. To her, none was unnecessary. Each served a purpose in her growing quest to understand her skin.

While other teenagers spent their pocket money on different interests, much of hers went towards skincare. She was particularly concerned with persistent breakouts, oily skin and the frustration of never quite achieving the clear complexion she wanted.

What her father saw as an unusually large collection of beauty products was, in retrospect, an early sign of an entrepreneurial journey to help herself and others understand and care for their skin.

Today, Umulisa is the founder and managing director of Pure Beauty Spa, a beauty and wellness business in Kigali’s Kimihurura neighborhood. What simply began as a teenager’s personal struggle with acne has evolved into a professional business.

When The Search for Clear Skin Became a Passion

In 2009, when she was in senior one at Ecole des Sciences Byimana, in Ruhango district, Umulisa became increasingly conscious of her appearance, as many teenagers do. Yet her relationship with her skin was particularly frustrating.

She had oily, acne-prone combination skin, a condition that made finding the right products and treatments difficult. Something would appear to work, only for another breakout to follow.

She wanted to understand why her skin behaved differently and why treatments did not always deliver the results she expected.

“I wanted to understand why I couldn’t have normal skin like everyone else. Why couldn’t I have clear skin like anyone else?” she recalls.

She began researching skincare, learning about different skin types, products and the science behind common skin problems. Gradually, she discovered that people have different types of skins that require different types of care.

Her interest deepened as she learned more about what caused acne, how the skin produces oil and why certain treatments work for some people but not others. The experience was so personal, that it quietly began shaping her future.

Beauty, meanwhile, was becoming a familiar part of her life in other ways. While still in school, she had a deal with her parents that good academic performance would earn her a special holiday treat, including having her hair done and her nails attended to.

It eventually became a family tradition. Every holiday, she looked forward to returning home and going to the salon. She remembers sitting in salons, sometimes without money of her own, imagining that one day she would own a place like that.

“I remember when I was in senior six, I didn’t even have anything in my account, but I would sit in the salon. I’m like, one day I’m going to own something like this,” she says.

It was a dream she carried for years, even as her understanding of beauty expanded beyond hairstyles and manicures to include skincare, treatments and wellness.

Turning Personal Curiosity into Professional Expertise

As her passion grew, Umulisa realized that understanding skincare required more than experimenting with products and conducting personal research. She wanted the professional knowledge to understand skin problems and offer treatments that could address them.

She pursued training in the field of aesthetic medicine, obtaining a diploma that strengthened her understanding of skincare and equipped her with skills to provide corrective treatments.

That knowledge also helped her appreciate why some skin conditions require more than medication or a single treatment.

At Pure Beauty Spa, which she founded on December 12, 2023, clients can access a range of services, including facials, chemical peels, micro needling, hydro facials, deep cleansing, hair treatments and nail care.

Her idea was to create a place where beauty and wellness could be experienced together rather than treated as separate services.

A client might visit for a haircut and discover other treatments suited to their needs, while the environment itself offers an opportunity to relax and take a break from everyday pressures.

For Umulisa, this approach is a broader expression of her passionate about helping people struggling with skin conditions, drawing on the frustrations she experienced as a teenager.

She explains that professional treatments can help address concerns such as acne scars, but results do not necessarily appear overnight. They require patience, appropriate home care and follow-up.

Her advice to clients includes maintaining a basic skincare routine involving cleansing, toning, moisturizing and, importantly, sunscreen.

She considers sunscreen indispensable, explaining that darker skin is not immune to the effects of ultraviolet radiation, sun damage and premature ageing.

Building the business has not been without challenges. Some clients expect immediate results from corrective treatments, while others struggle to appreciate the difference between the price of a service and the quality of products, expertise and care behind it.

Umulisa says educating clients about the time required for treatments to work has become part of running the business. She remains particularly firm on maintaining service quality, even as she navigates customers’ different expectations.

Since inception, Pure Beauty Spa has experienced growth in its services and customer engagement, a feat she describes as increasing interest in beauty and wellness treatments in Kigali.

Yet she is not content with what has been achieved so far. Her ambition is to expand beyond the capital and make professional beauty and wellness services accessible to more people across Rwanda.

For someone who once spent her pocket money trying to understand her own skin and sat in salons imagining a business she could one day own, the journey is surely a fulfilment of a precious childhood ambition.

But Umulisa sees the business as only one part of a bigger purpose of encouraging people to make self-care a meaningful part of their lives.

The girl who once filled her bedroom with skincare products in search of answers has built a place where others come looking for care, confidence and relaxation.

And, much like the passion that first took root in her teenage years, she believes the dream is still growing.

Trump initially asked the UFC boss to be press secretary on Saturday

US President Donald Trump has said he "was kidding" about asking Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be the White House press secretary.

Trump told the media on Sunday that White "loves the idea" but that the invitation was "just a little fun".

It comes after the president posted on his Truth Social platform on Saturday that he had offered White the role, asking him to take it while writing, "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other."

White said later that day he was going to meet the president on Monday, but would not be drawn into whether or not he would take the vacant position.

On Sunday Trump told reporters White was visiting him on Monday for "other reasons".

"I think he's going to be in Washington. So he's going to come over and see me.

"I will tell you, I was only kidding. But Dana loves the idea. And there's only one Dana. He's great," the president said.

The press secretary role is yet to be filled after it became vacant in October when Katie Zacharia quit after less than five days in the job .

She took over from Karoline Leavitt, who was the youngest press secretary in US history and had held the role since Trump began his second term.

Trump's job offer came after a heavy loss in the midterm elections, where the Republican Party lost its majority in both houses of Congress.

In his Truth Social post on Saturday, he said he was "pleased to announce" that White "has been offered the job".

He said he had asked White to bring with him several current and former mixed martial arts fighters as "assistants".

"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," he wrote.

Asked about the Trump offer at a news conference on Saturday, the UFC chief executive said he had "lot of jobs already" .

"I'm sure we'll have something to talk about after that," he said of their planned Monday meeting, but did not say whether or not he would take the job.

White leads UFC, and PowerSlap, a regulated slap-fighting promotion league, as well as recently launching promotion company Zuffa Boxing.

He is also a board member of Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

White appeared as a speaker in support of Trump's White House campaigns at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

He also appeared on stage for Trump's victory speech in the 2024 presidential election.

This summer, the UFC staged a cage match on the White House lawn.

Fears are mounting of Ebola spreading after a deadly attack conducted by the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) rebels against civilians in the Cantine area of Beni territory, North Kivu.

According to local reports from the area the attack, occurred on the night of Thursday, November 5, to Friday, November 6.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) warned of the consequences of the violence on the response to the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the region.

The organization said it was concerned about the attacks on health facilities and the fleeing of hundreds of patients, some with confirmed or suspected Ebola infection, in search of safety.

“The Africa-CDC strongly condemns the deadly attack perpetrated against civilians in Cantine-Aloya, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), on November 5, 2026, which was allegedly carried out by the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF),” statement reads in part.

The organization added, “During an Ebola outbreak, any disruption to patient care, contact tracing, and disease surveillance creates additional risks for communities already facing exceptional challenges.”

“Populations must be able to access care safely, and health workers must be able to provide essential services without fear of violence.”

Africa CDC calls for the establishment of a peace corridor, the protection of civilians, patients, healthcare workers and facilities, and safe and sustainable access to affected communities.

All parties must respect the protection afforded to healthcare under international humanitarian law.

Dr. Jean Kaseya, Executive Director of Africa CDC, emphasized the additional risks that any disruption to care, contact tracing, and epidemiological surveillance poses to communities already grappling with the epidemic.

“I am deeply saddened and outraged by the deadly attack perpetrated against civilians in Cantine-Aloya, North Kivu, DRC. My thoughts are with the families who have lost loved ones and with all the communities affected by this violence,” Kaseya said.

Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders estimates that for every 100 people who reach the Canary Islands by sea, 21 die during the crossing (file photo)

At least 39 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports.

The interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.

The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.

Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.

Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told the AFP news agency that all the bodies recovered by Sunday evening were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.

Four bodies were recovered on Monday morning in an advanced state of decomposition and buried following a collective funeral prayer organised by the fire service.

Rescue teams are searching along a 25km (15-mile)- stretch of coastline, but operations have been complicated by difficult access and strong ocean currents, which are pushing bodies further south.

Authorities say 24 of the 39 victims have been identified and their bodies returned to their families, while 11 others are still awaiting identification.

President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not to risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.

In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys.

"We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.

The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.

Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.

Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.

Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.

Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.

More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.

This amounts to almost a third of the population on the island, one of the main entry points into Europe for migrants arriving from West Africa.

Fernando Clavijo, president of the Canary Islands regional government, described the situation as "absolutely unsustainable," reports the Reuters news agency.

The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.

Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.

Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.

The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.

In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.

Fans of Vitesse Arnhem celebrated an absence of away fans in the 2025-26 edition of their home match with De Graafschap

A Dutch second-tier match between Vitesse Arnhem and De Graafschap was called off after away team supporters blocked their own team's bus from departing for the game.

Fans of De Graafschap were protesting the decision to ban away fans from attending the game at Vitesse's GelreDome stadium after supporters had not agreed to security measures set out for the derby fixture.

Reports in Dutch media said De Graafschap fans gathered outside their stadium in Doetinchem early on Sunday and blocked the bus from leaving.

The Dutch Football Association said in a statement that the match would not go ahead on Sunday and that the matter would be referred to the disciplinary bodies.

"It is an unacceptable situation that the Vitesse - De Graafschap match cannot go ahead in this way. That supporters making football impossible is completely intolerable," it said.

"In doing so, they harm their club, their team, the sport, and the thousands of supporters who do come for the football."

In a Saturday statement , external , Vitesse announced that they had made the decision to ban away fans "based on police information and after extensive consultation with all involved security partners."

They had proposed an away fans allocation of 500 - cut from the standard 800 - dependent on a number of security measures including "fan paraphernalia brought along had to be subject to inspection prior to the supporters' arrival."

"Over the past few weeks, Vitesse, the police, and the municipality have repeatedly offered De Graafschap various options to meet these conditions.

"However, police information and conversations with De Graafschap indicate that a portion of the supporters is insisting on bringing fan paraphernalia in a manner contrary to the agreements made."

Vitesse added their decision had been made in light of "serious disturbances" surrounding the 2025-26 edition of the fixture, from which De Graafschap supporters were also banned.

In their response to the announcement , external , De Graafschap said they did "not recognize the picture painted by the Arnhem press release regarding the commitment and stance of our club and our supporters.

"As a club, we find it unacceptable that our supporters are portrayed in this manner."

Responding to the cancellation Vitesse director Willem van der Linden said the cancellation was a "major disappointment".

"A wonderful Gelderland derby between two regional clubs, in a well-filled stadium, could not go ahead today," he wrote in a letter posted on the club's website , external .

"In the run-up to the match, Vitesse, in close cooperation with all parties involved, did everything possible to still get the match started."

De Graafschap said in a statement on social media that they were "shocked by the incident" and "want to let the initial emotion subside and get a full picture of everything before we come with a further substantive response."

A new date for the fixture is yet to be announced, but Van der Linden said the intention was to hold the game "under the same circumstances."

Vitesse are 10th after the weekend's fixtures while De Graafschap, who play less than 20 miles to the east of their rivals, sit in 15th.

Inyubako ya Aramco Tower, imwe mu nzu ndende ziherereye mu gice cy'ubucuruzi n'imari rwagati mu murwa mukuru wa Arabiya Sawudite, Riyadh, yatewe n'igitero cyagabwe mu kirere.

Mu itangazo ryasohowe n'ibiro ntaramakuru Saba, biyobowe n'umutwe w'Aba-Houthi, uyu mutwe wemeje ko wagabye igitero ku gace k'ubucuruzi ka Riyadh ku wa gatandatu, n'ubwo utigeze uvuga izina rya Aramco Tower.

Minisiteri y'ingufu ya Arabiya Sawudite yatangaje ko iyo nyubako yangiritseho bike gusa kandi ko nta muntu wapfuye cyangwa ngo habe hari uwakomeretse.

Amashusho yagenzuwe na BBC Verify agaragaza ko inyubako yangiritse cyane kurushaho, aho nibura igorofa imwe igaragara nk'iyangijwe bikomeye n'igisasu cya misile cyangwa indege nto itagira umupilote (drone).

Amadirishya yo ku magorofa arenze imwe na yo yasadutse kubera icyo gitero.

Aba-Houthi bavuga kandi ko ikibuga cy'indege cya Riyadh n'ibigega bibikamo peteroli bya Aramco na byo byagabweho ibindi bitero bitandukanye.

Arabiya Sawudite yo yatangaje ko ubwirinzi bwayo bwo mu kirere bwashoboye gufata no kurasa misile nyinshi mbere y'uko zigera ku ntego zazo.

Ibi bitero ni bimwe mu biheruka uyu mutwe witwaje intwaro ukorera muri Yemen uvuga ko wagabye ku bikorwa remezo biri imbere muri Arabiya Sawudite, igihugu cyakomeje kugorwa no kubihagarika mu mezi ashize.

Ibi byabaye nyuma y'umunsi umwe Aba-Houthi bashinje ihuriro ry'ibihugu riyobowe na Arabiya Sawudite kwica nibura abantu 33, harimo abagore n'abana, mu gitero cy'indege cyagabwe muri Yemen.

Amashusho yatambukijwe na televiziyo Al Masirah, icungwa n'Aba-Houthi, yerekanaga abatabazi bakura imirambo munsi y'ibisigazwa by'inyubako nyinshi mu mujyi wa al-Shariyah, uherereye mu burasirazuba bw'umurwa mukuru Sanaa.

Ibiro ntaramakuru Saba byatangaje ko abantu 39 bakomerekeye muri icyo gitero. Arabiya Sawudite ntiyari yagira icyo ikivugaho.

Ihuriro ry'ibihugu riyobowe na Arabiya Sawudite rimaze imyaka isaga icumi rirwana n'Aba-Houthi mu gushyigikira guverinoma ya Yemen, yamaze gutakaza ububasha ku gice kinini cy'igihugu.

N'ubwo intambara yari yaracogoye mu myaka ishize, imirwano yongeye gukara nyuma y'itangira ry'intambara ya Iran.

Agahenge katari kanditse ku mpapuro karasenyutse muri Nyakanga(7), nyuma y'uko Aba-Houthi bashyizeho icyo bise "gukumira ibikorwa byo mu nyanja" bya Arabiya Sawudite, maze bagatangira kugaba ibitero bya misile na drone ku bibuga by'indege, ibikorwa bya peteroli n'amato atwara peteroli mu nyanja itukura.

Aba-Houthi bavuga ko bari kwihorera ku byo bise gukumirwa kw'uturere bagenzura na Arabiya Sawudite, ndetse no ku gitero cyagabwe ku kibuga cy'indege cya Sanaa, Arabiya Sawudite ikavuga ko cyari kigamije gukumira indege yo muri Iran kukigwaho.

Kuva icyo gihe, imirwano ikomeye yongeye kubura hagati y'ingabo z'Aba-Houthi n'izishyigikiye guverinoma ya Yemen ifashwa na Arabiya Sawudite.

Umuryango w'Abibumbye uvuga ko kuva imirwano yongeye kubura, abarenga 1,600 bamaze kwicwa, naho abarenga 300,000 bo bavuye mu byabo.

Kenyan police have seized 454kg (1,000lb) of methamphetamine worth an estimated $27m (£20m) in an operation targeting international drug trafficking networks.

Three suspects, two Tanzanians and a Ugandan, were arrested at the Kenyan coast following an intelligence-led operation involving Kenyan anti-narcotics officers and their Tanzanian counterparts.

Police said the investigations began after a key suspect was arrested in Tanzania last week and handed over to Kenyan authorities at the border.

Methamphetamine, commonly known as meth, is a harmful illegal synthetic drug that is highly addictive and can lead to severe psychosis, heart attack or stroke.

The haul is one of the largest drug seizures in Kenya's history.

The suspect, who was allegedly linked to a separate seizure of 299kg of suspected methamphetamine and heroin in Tanzania, led officers to a location in Msambweni on the Kenyan coast, where the drug haul was discovered.

Police made further arrests at the site and seized two motor vehicles and a motorcycle.

Aretas Lyimo, head of Tanzania's Drug Control and Enforcement Authority (DCEA), says initial questioning indicated that the drugs found in Tanzania had come through the Kenyan port of Mombasa.

He added that investigations suggested that some of those arrested were key figures in an international drug trafficking network operating across several countries, including Afghanistan, South Africa, Mozambique, Zambia, Malawi, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania and UAE.

A total of seven suspects were arrested in the two locations, five Tanzanians and two Ugandans, he said.

The four suspects in Kenya are currently in custody and due to be arraigned in court, while the recovered narcotics and the seized items are being kept as exhibits.

The police say the operation remains ongoing and urged members of the public to to share information that will help tackle drug trafficking.

Last month, Kenya's Deputy President Kithure Kindiki declared illicit alcohol and drug abuse to be among the country's top threats.

He warned that the government would introduce tougher laws and intensify nationwide operations to deal with the menace.

In a separate operation last month, authorities destroyed more than a tonne of methamphetamine from a consignment intercepted last year by the Kenyan navy about 630km (390 miles) off the Mombasa coast.

The Institute for Security Studies, a think-tank, has warned of a shift in East Africa's role in international drug trafficking.

It says the region's coastline is increasingly becoming not just a transit route for drugs destined for other markets but also an entry point for manufactured drugs intended for local consumption.

From Western Europe to Indonesia, countries have battled wildfires throughout 2026 following record heat from climate change and El Niño

The world is on course for its hottest year on record as the planet is hit with warming from climate change and El Niño, scientists have told BBC News.

The warning comes as world leaders and negotiators gather in Turkey on Monday for the opening of COP31, the latest UN climate summit.

Berkeley Earth, the independent US research group behind the forecast, said that even with two months of the year left it is 95% confident that 2026 will surpass the previous record set in 2024.

The impact of rising heat has been felt acutely in recent months by countries attending COP, with extensive wildfires across Europe and the sudden glacier collapse in Nepal which killed more than 1,000 people.

"We have had a run of record warm years," said Dr Robert Rohde, of Berkeley Earth. "That is what we expect as global warming progresses… glaciers collapsing, record-breaking heatwaves and droughts."

On Friday, the EU's Copernicus climate service , external confirmed that October was the hottest on record.

But Rohde warned this was just the start. "There is potential for much larger and much more dramatic changes down the line," he said.

The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

The UN's World Meteorological Organization (WMO) published its own report on Monday , external , and although more cautious than Berkeley, it has forecast that 2026 will be among the four warmest years on record.

It said that 2027 will provide no let-up, as an unusually powerful El Niño will continue into next year, pushing temperatures higher.

WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said it "gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts".

The findings underline the challenge facing negotiators gathering in the seaside Turkish city of Antalya for COP31.

At previous meetings the focus has been on reducing emissions - tackling the cause of climate change. But now an increasing number of nations are facing the reality of having to do that alongside adapting to new weather extremes as the planet warms.

"No single COP is a silver bullet. No single conference can bridge the chasm between the science and reality," Simon Stiell, the UN's climate chief, said as he addressed delegates on the opening morning.

But he added "the urgency of this moment must drive us forward. Global heating is already costing the Earth."

Last month the UK defence secretary warned the public and businesses to think about how they would cope with increasing natural disasters, including stockpiling food.

Prepare for supply chain disruption from climate emergencies, Streeting warns

Wes Streeting pointed to wildfires this summer and record heat, which the Met Office has said was made 130 times more likely by climate change , as well as increased risk of flooding this winter as a result of El Niño.

Stephen Belcher, chief scientist at the Met Office, told BBC's Panorama: "We're designed for a climate of the 20th century that we don't live in any longer, so it's going to change all aspects of our lives."

The BBC's climate editor, Justin Rowlatt, investigates the impact of the changing climate on our weather.

Watch on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One (BBC Two in Northern Ireland) at 20:00 on Monday 9 November.

The additional greenhouse gases being added to the atmosphere have trapped additional heat and about 90% of that has been absorbed by the oceans.

That's where El Niño comes in, said Saulo. "It doesn't add new heat to the planet. It releases heat from the ocean, which is the warmest ever measured. There is simply more heat available to release."

This natural climate pattern is pushing global temperatures even higher.

The world is currently on track for 2.8C of warming , external above pre-industrial levels by the end of the century - all but guaranteed to exceed the goal of 1.5C set under the Paris Agreement to avoid the worst effects of climate change.

Listen now on BBC sounds: Climate overshoot: The world beyond 1.5°C

Countries will negotiate for two weeks with leaders, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham, attending the conference this week.

Previous climate summits have yielded new targets for countries to follow on cutting fossil fuels, increasing money for developing countries and protections for forests.

Although emissions continue to increase, countries have also made significant progress in increasing renewable energy capacity. The International Energy Agency has predicted , external growth in the next six years will be 57% greater than the previous period.

Stiell also said that expanding renewable energy was both a climate and economic solution for recent energy shocks. "Global renewables saved around half a trillion dollars last year."

China remains the largest contributor to the global increase in renewable power capacity but that will decline as other developing nations expand

The Turkish government says it wants discussions this year to focus on a new goal for electrification - moving energy systems away from fossil fuels towards electricity - and cutting waste levels.

But the discussion is likely to split countries.

Early drafts of the EU position seen by the BBC make clear they would only sign up to a goal on electrification if it did not allow countries to meet the target using gas.

"It is important that progress on electrification is underpinned by clean energy sources," it said in a memo to members.

But nations, such as Saudi Arabia and Russia, have previously pushed the interim use of gas as a "cleaner" fossil fuel alternative to coal.

Previous COP negotiations have struggled to get agreement on phasing out fossil fuels

Celeste Saulo of the WMO said she could not offer an explanation as to why countries have previously not reached agreement on certain issues, but said "what I see are the impacts of what this lack of consensus generates with more extreme events".

The BBC understands that the UK government is reluctant to set any new goals at COP31 and thinks the focus should be on achieving existing agreements.

But, on Monday it was reported that the UK government's electric vehicle (EV) targets are expected to be reduced in a move that risks the country's long-term climate goals, according to sustainability groups.

And in September the government was criticised by MPs on the International Development Committee , external for cutting its aid budget meaning it could not fulfil previous climate funding commitments.

Wealthier nations had agreed at previous COP meetings to triple the amount of money going to developing countries to help them adapt to climate change to at least $85bn (£63bn) by 2035.

The latest data from 2024 shows that countries have reached about a third of that figure, but the UN said this week that the current damage from climate change being experienced is "substantial" and much more money could be needed.

But many countries have redirected aid budgets towards defence spending and short-term financial relief for households as gas and oil prices spike following the Iran-US war.

Governments are also expected to use the forum to discuss global AI policy including the growing demand for energy and water resources from data centres underpinning the technology's rollout.

A gunman suspected of killing six people in central Krakow, as well as his parents and sister at their home, died in hospital early on Monday, Polish police have said.

The 24-year-old, who has been named as Michal Oksinski by local media, was injured after opening fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland, on Saturday, police said.

Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.

Authorities initially reported that the gunman had apparently been inspired by "far-right ideologies", but have since said they are investigating any possible motivation.

After the shooting, which began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's busy Main Market Square, police identified the attacker as a 24-year-old Polish man.

In the hours after the shooting, a minister said that early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.

However, during a press briefing on Monday morning, Przemysław Nowak, a spokesperson for Poland's National Prosecutor's Office, said investigations into his motive remain ongoing.

Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed in the attack.

People run for shelter as gunshots heard in Krakow

Four victims are Polish, while a British national and an Austrian woman were also killed.

Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack.

On Sunday, Polish police confirmed those three victims had been identified as the alleged gunman's 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and 21-year-old sister.

Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.

Four firearms were found in the gunman's car, including two AR-15 rifles and two handguns, along with several hundred rounds of ammunition, Nowak said. Authorities also seized at least four phones from his car and person, and electronic equipment from his home.

Sixteen people, including five foreigners, two police officers and the attacker, were taken to hospital. The interior ministry later said they were from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia.

Speaking on Sunday, one of two surgeons who treated victims on the street after the attack said his colleague "undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.

The two surgeons, who were eating near the Main Market Square when the gunman opened fire, rushed to the scene to treat both the attacker and the two injured police officers.

Watch: Doctor who treated victims of Krakow shooting speaks to the BBC

Professor Michal Pędziwiatr told the BBC: "We saw the shooting attack. And what a surgeon can do in a situation like this?... We decided to help the victims as soon as possible."

"We rushed into the area where the shooting was and started our rescue, because there were no ambulances available, there were no professionals around."

Pędziwiatr said his colleague, who has been named by local media as Dr Mateusz Wierdak, used his hand to stem the bleeding from the most severely injured policeman, allowing time for an ambulance to arrive.

On Sunday it was reported that both injured officers had emerged from comas.

Witnesses who were near the Main Market Square have described their panic and confusion as the attack unfolded.

Ruby, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".

She said they "just kept sprinting" until they found a hotel to shelter inside.

Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover".

"I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 metres away," he said.

In the wake of the shooting, Poland declared the country would enter two days of national mourning.

After travelling to Krakow, Tusk said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism...that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków".

"My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.

Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.
