The government launched a review into its policy to ban new petrol and diesel car sales by 2035

The UK government's electric vehicle (EV) targets are expected to be reduced this week in a move likely to be welcomed by carmakers but opposed by environmental groups.

Under the current rules, 80% of new cars sold in the UK must be electric by 2030 but industry groups have long called for "urgent relief".

New petrol or diesel cars are due to be phased out by 2030 and by 2035 all new cars must be zero emission.

But the speed of the transition to electric has been hotly debated, including within the cabinet.

The government has been consulting on reducing its 80% rule and a significant reduction is now expected.

Downing Street has insisted no decision has been made.

A government source told the BBC it would approach the issue in a "pragmatic and balanced" way.

If ministers do decide on a steeper watering-down of the rules, it will arguably be interpreted by some - alongside the approval of the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea - as the government prioritising economic considerations over environmental ones.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has recused himself from this issue due to his wife's links to an electric vehicle company.

The key meetings on the subject will instead be chaired by Cabinet Office minister Louise Haigh.

Asked about reports the targets would be reduced, Burnham dismissed this as "speculation", adding: "No decision has been made at this point."

Sustainability groups say any weakening of the 2030 target will threaten the UK's long-term electrification and climate goals.

It could undermine the UK's claim to be providing leadership on climate just as ministers head to Turkey for COP31, the UN's climate summit.

Energy UK, the trade association for the energy industry, has also opposed the move.

Last month, it said , external reducing targets could damage "the investment certainty needed to deliver the infrastructure, innovation and services required for the transition to zero-emission transport".

Asked if climate change was no longer a big priority, Health Minister Karin Smyth said the government was committed to its emissions targets.

"This country is doing great work in terms of our transition and looking at renewables – that's a key part of growth in different parts of the country," she told BBC Breakfast.

She added that the prime minister would have "a good story to tell" when meeting other leaders at COP31.

A government spokesperson said: "We are committed to the phase out of all new cars relying solely on petrol and diesel engines by 2030, and to 100% of new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, and our legally binding net zero targets."

The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders welcomed the government's review of the EV targets when it was announced in the summer.

Last week, head of the association Mike Hawes said transitioning to electric vehicles had come at a "heavy cost" with billions spent on discounts to drive demand in electric vehicles.

He said the government's targets could not be achieved "without putting at risk any future investment".

UK electric car sales target set to be weakened

Electric vehicle sales targets could be cut after pressure from car makers

EU waters down plans to end new petrol and diesel car sales by 2035

Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.

The government's policy to phase out petrol and diesel vehicle sales has undergone multiple changes since it was first introduced by former Prime Minister Boris Johnson in 2020.

His successor Rishi Sunak pushed back the timeline to 2035, and the Burnham government set up a review of the EV sales targets in August.

Sunak introduced phased targets for EV sales in the UK, known as the Zero Emission Vehicles (ZEV) mandate.

Under the ZEV mandate, the percentage of new car sales that need to be EVs increases each year. The target was 28% for 2025, 33% for 2026, and so on until it reaches 80% by 2030.

Pressure in the European Union saw the bloc scrap a similar plan to ban new petrol and diesel car sales by 2035, particularly from countries with large auto industries such as Germany.

The Conservative Party has also vowed to abandon the petrol car ban if it wins the next election, with leader Kemi Badenoch calling it a "well-meaning, but ultimately destructive piece of legislation".

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said the government was "building up a shocking record of backsliding and bad decisions on climate issues".

Daniel Craig (pictured with co-star Léa Seydoux) stepped down as Bond with 2021's No Time To Die

When a bartender asked James Bond in 2006's Casino Royale whether he'd like his vodka martini shaken or stirred, the irritated spy replied: "Do I look like I give a damn?"

Such throwaway lines were a clever way of signalling to the audience that this was a new era for 007 - and that the film series launched in 1962 was being overhauled with the arrival of Daniel Craig.

Over the next few films, producers struck a balance between nodding to the past while also moving away from some of the cheesier elements of the series, no longer sticking rigidly to all of the tradition and tropes of Bond.

"Were you expecting an exploding pen?" Ben Whishaw's Q later asked the secret service agent in Skyfall. "We don't really go in for that anymore."

Two decades on from Craig's debut, the series is about to be rebooted once again, with a new actor and new creative team. It's an exciting time for Bond fans as they wait to see what shape the next era will take. Here's what we know so far.

L-R: Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Jack Barton are all thought to have auditioned for the role

After years of speculation, the wheels are firmly in motion and we expect to hear who the new James Bond actor is in November or December.

Speaking in August, producer Amy Pascal told Deadline: , external "I would say the end of the year is a good bet. We are being really, really methodical."

The final screen tests reportedly took place in late October, so, unless something unexpected happens, it should not take much longer for producers to make their decision and the actor to sign the contract.

After that, it's just a matter of how the announcement will be made. In an earlier era, Bond actors were revealed with a traditional photo call or press conference.

But now that the franchise is owned by Amazon MGM, some expect the company to make the announcement via its own Prime Video streaming service.

Josh O'Connor starred opposite previous Bond actor Daniel Craig in Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery

A handful of actors are thought to have made it to the final screen tests to take on Britain's biggest film role. The three frontrunners are thought to be:

Jack Lowden , 36 - whose credits include Slow Horses and Pride and Prejudice

Josh O'Connor , 36 - The Crown, Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery

Callum Turner , 36 - Masters of the Air, The Capture

Jack Barton , 31 - Heartstopper, SAS: Rogue Heroes

Nicholas Hoult , 36 - About A Boy, Superman

Robert Pattinson , 40 - Twilight, The Batman

Paul Mescal , 30 - Normal People, Gladiator II

But remember, Craig was a surprise choice in 2005, so don't bet against a wildcard candidate whose name has not yet been widely reported.

The film is expected to go into production in 2027, before its release in 2028. No exact dates have been announced.

Film schedules can be notoriously fluid, but it's clear that development is well under way, with the director and writer already in place.

It will be the 26th film in the official film series, but the title has not yet been confirmed.

Steven Knight (left) will write the script, while Denis Villeneuve will direct the film

The movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve , known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival, Blade Runner 2049 and the recent Dune trilogy starring Timothée Chalamet.

"Some of my earliest movie-going memories are connected to 007," the French-Canadian director said last year. "I grew up watching James Bond films with my father, ever since Dr. No with Sean Connery. I'm a die-hard Bond fan. To me, he's sacred territory."

He added: "I intend to honour the tradition and open the path for many new missions to come. This is a massive responsibility, but also, incredibly exciting for me and a huge honour."

Bond 26 will be written by Steven Knight , known for TV series such as Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke and The Girl in the Spider's Web.

Knight has said it had always been on his "bucket list" to write a Bond film, adding that he felt he was "doing my duty for King and country" by joining the franchise.

He told the BBC he planned to "write the character, not the actor", adding: "The thing with Bond is it's its own universe and franchise. So there are certain rules.

"Obviously you have to move it along, but I love where it sits. I love that it's British. I love that it's not DC or Marvel... So I feel a responsibility to the text."

Irish actor Pierce Brosnan starred in four Bond films, including 1999's The World Is Not Enough

Sean Connery starred in six official Bond films between 1962 and 1971

George Lazenby starred in just one Bond film, in 1969

Roger Moore starred in seven Bond films between 1973 and 1985

Timothy Dalton starred in two Bond films, in 1987 and 1989

Pierce Brosnan starred in four Bond films, between 1995 and 2002

Daniel Craig starred in five Bond films between 2006 and 2021

You might have noticed some overlap in the above dates.

That's because Connery returned to the lead role for 1971's Diamonds Are Forever, after Lazenby took his place for 1969's On Her Majesty's Secret Service.

Connery also later appeared in 1983's Never Say Never Again, a Bond film produced by a different studio and not part of the official film series.

Roger Moore pictured filming 1985's A View To A Kill

If you discount the films not in the official series, there have been 25 Bond films in total. In order, they are:

At the 2005 press call announcing him as the new Bond, Daniel Craig arrived by boat with the Royal Marines

With the change in ownership and a new creative team now in place, the new Bond film is likely to make a fresh start.

It would be difficult to continue the story chronologically given the ending of 2021's No Time To Die, but that still leaves producers with plenty of options.

A different version of James Bond, who exists in a different universe, would be easily pulled off in an era where audiences are used to major film franchises restarting in a different world or timeline.

Bond 26 could even be set in a significantly earlier era - an idea that gained more popularity after Tony Gilroy revealed he and fellow director Steven Soderbergh previously pitched a 1960s version , external of Bond.

Separately, actor Ralph Fiennes recently said , external he had once been in talks to play Bond, and had suggested producers make a "black and white and very sort of film noir-y" version set in the 1950s.

Neither idea materialised, but the suggestion went down well with some Bond fans, who noted a period piece would help make the film truer to Ian Fleming's original character and books.

Exactly what shape the next film takes will become clear at a later stage. For now, fans are hoping that Christmas could be about to come early this year, as the world awaits the imminent announcement of the next actor to play 007.

Jess Fishlock won more caps and scored more goals for Wales than any other player, male or female

Wales legend Jess Fishlock's playing career is over, after Seattle Reign were beaten 1-0 by Gotham FC in the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) play-off quarter-finals.

The 39-year-old midfielder began her career with home town club Cardiff City in 2002. She played in eight different countries and collected Champions League winners medals with FFC Frankfurt and Olympique Lyonnais.

Fishlock retired from international football in October 2025 after scoring 48 times in 166 international appearances - both Wales records.

She won three NWSL Shields during a 14-season stint with Seattle but announced in April this season would be her last.

"I've loved it," said an emotional Fishlock, as she wiped away tears after losing to Gotham on Sunday.

"And the truth is I've loved that my last year was with this group, because they have just given me so much, and not just on the field."

Fishlock will now be part of Rhian Wilkinson's Wales coaching staff for December's two-leg World Cup play-off against Norway.

Wales face Denmark and Italy again on League A return

Wales in fight to retain rising female stars

Fishlock, who has previously held player-coach roles at Cardiff City Ladies and Melbourne Victory, joined Seattle for the inaugural NWSL season in 2013.

Reign finished eighth in this year's regular season table to claim the final play-off berth, and they pushed number one seed Gotham close in a game during which Fishlock left the field in the 74th minute.

"Two years ago I was just 'I can't work with these kids', as in I'm too old for it, but they have given me just so much joy," added Fishlock.

"And obviously the older ones, we've just had to rely on each other so much these last couple of years and it's created deeper relationships within what we've already been doing, and because of that I've seen so much growth on and off the field from this team.

"So even today I'm not upset that I'll never play football again - I'm ok with that, I've played enough - but I am devastated that I will not get to spend more time with this group because they will win."

Reign defender Sofia Huerta said it had been a privelege to play with Fishlock, who she described as the best player she had ever seen.

"She came into this league and it was so lucky to have her," said Huerta. "She put this league on the map.

"Playing with Jess has been my greatest honour. I've seen her be the best professional, such a good player, but the best thing about Jess is she's just such a good person."

Jess Fishlock's emotional final press conference as a player

Fishlock helped Wales' women qualify for their first major finals in 2025, becoming the oldest scorer at a Women's European Championship in the 4-1 defeat by France.

However, she said it would not be easy to pick out one memory as a snapshot of her career.

"I look back and there's just so much to think about, not only with Reign but with Wales," mused Fishlock.

"It would have to be one of those panorama snapshots because it's too difficult.

"All I know is what I'm most proud of deeply in my soul is that... I've stayed with Wales - that was difficult for 20 years, wouldn't do it any other way - stayed with the Reign for 14 years, wouldn't do it any other way.

"Because for me, when you win with your people - with the people that you've struggled with, the people that you've lost with, the people that you've failed with - when you win with your people, there is no better feeling in the world."

Former Wales captain Kath Morgan, who coached Fishlock from the age of nine, told BBC Radio Wales' Breakfast programme the midfielder is the best player to have to come out of Wales.

And while Fishlock played for Bristol Academy in the early years of the Women's Super League (WSL) - winning the league's player's player of the year award in 2012 - and had a spell on loan at Reading during Seattle's off-season in 2020, Morgan believes England's top-flight missed out on a generational talent.

"For me, the telling point is that Jess has played all over the world, and you have to be a good player to get away with that," said Morgan.

"The only thing I would say is that the WSL has massively missed out on Jess's presence, which for me is a little bit disappointing.

"I think it was probably the wrong time, and she'd already kind of decided that she was going to settle over in Seattle, and she was happy there... obviously we've got to respect that, but it's just a shame."

Komtek I (left) was created in 1962 from an early computer image

A print by a Yorkshire artist commissioned by Nasa in the early days of space travel will go on show as part of a pop art exhibition.

Komtek I by Michael Fossick, who studied at Bradford School of Art, was created in 1962 to celebrate a Hong Kong company that produced microcomputers in the early days of space travel.

The print was part of a Nasa project to document the effort of sending the first humans to the moon and is on display as part of the Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition.

The display tells the story of the British International Print Biennale, which took place at the Bradford gallery on 11 occasions between 1968 and 1990, and runs until March 2027.

While the exhibition also includes work by Andy Warhol and David Hockney, there is "definitely stuff that people won't have seen before", said curator Jill Iredale.

"It's a completely bizarre sort of connection somehow that an artist born in Sheffield that went to Bradford School of Art was somehow commissioned by Nasa," said Iredale.

"It was actually a screen print, but it was made from a very early computerised image," she said.

In March 1962, Nasa administrator James Webb awarded commissions to 38 artists, including Fossick, to document the space agency's achievements.

John H. Glenn became the first American to orbit the earth on 20 February 1962 and in the following decade Nasa's Mercury programme led to the Apollo missions, and eventually to Neil Armstrong setting foot on the moon in 1969.

Fossick chose to honour Komtek I, a microcomputer produced by Komtek Technologies Ltd in Hong Kong that was significant in the early years of the space programme.

He submitted the print to the First British International Print Biennale held at Cartwright Hall in 1968 where it won a prize.

Cartwright Hall is home to one of Andy Warhol's famous Marilyn prints

Created by a group of local print makers and artists, at its height the British International Print Biennale included more than 500 works selected from more than 3,000 entries.

It received work by artists such as Andy Warhol, Roy Licthenstein and David Hockney, which remain in the gallery today.

Hockney was invited to be a judge on the first biennial in 1968 and created the poster for the show, which is on display in the exhibition.

Iredale said the pop art explosion in Bradford was a reaction to the seriousness of the World War Two and the boost in commercial print culture.

"Bradford had quite a strong, experimental kind of light, pretty kind of DIY aesthetic with artists and with the college as well," she explained.

"There was simply loads more young people around, post-baby boom, and an increase in opportunities for working-class youth."

Michael Ball attended Dave and Dawn Lloyd's wedding ceremony on Sunday

A couple whose surprise radio proposal captured hearts across the country were given an unforgettable wedding gift when singer and broadcaster Michael Ball turned up to perform at their ceremony.

Dawn Lloyd was shocked when her partner of more than 25 years Dave proposed on BBC Radio 2's Love Songs with Michael Ball programme in the summer and was stunned all over again when the presenter appeared at the couple's wedding at Weston Hall, in Stafford, on Sunday.

"I had no inkling whatsoever that this was going to happen," she said. "I was blown away.

"I just can't believe Dave has surprised me like this a second time. I was fooled the first time and now he has got me again."

Ball appeared without warning during the ceremony and performed Love Changes Everything, leaving Dawn and the wedding guests stunned.

Dawn said the day had been "perfect", with Dave adding he was "grateful for what Michael has done for us as a couple and for all of the family and friends to enjoy it as well".

Dave said he was "grateful for what Michael has done for us as a couple"

Dave and Dawn, from Cannock, won over listeners when Dave secretly teamed up with Ball to stage the proposal.

Dawn, believing she was taking part in a BBC tour, was welcomed into the studio by Ball, who pretended he was recording voiceovers, before Dave read out a love letter and proposed to the woman he had been with for 31 years.

During the broadcast, Dave revealed he had already booked the wedding at Weston Hall, choosing a date close to 11 November, the anniversary of the day they first got together.

Ball later said the proposal was "so moving" that "we thought we have to follow this through".

Weston Hall holds special significance for the couple and was where Dave first proposed in the late 1990s.

But Dawn, who was 19 at the time, was so overwhelmed that she laughed, and the engagement ring was later lost, meaning the engagement never officially stuck.

More than 25 years later, the couple, who now have three children, finally made it down the aisle at the venue where their story began.

Gen Phoenix in Peterborough transforms leather offcuts into a new lower-carbon fabric, used by brands such as Dr Martens and Coach

How many clothes, items of bedding and other fabric have you thrown away this year?

While resale sites are growing in popularity, in the UK we still bin about 711,000 tonnes of textiles annually , external – roughly the weight of seven US aircraft carriers , external .

The global fashion and textiles industry is one of the most wasteful, but recycling firms in Peterborough and Northamptonshire are using technology to change that.

They are gaining the attention of major brands but say they need laws, as well as consumers, to support them.

New EU legislation requires fashion brands on sale there to demonstrate the sustainability of their products

In a warehouse next to the A14 in Kettering, a mountain of crumpled fabric is slowly fed into a machine.

There are dressing gowns, duvets, branded banners and lanyards from events including the Commonwealth Games.

All are made from polyester – the world's most commonly used textile fibre – and all have been thrown away.

Traditionally they would be burned or buried in landfill but Project Re:Claim is trying to change that.

The partnership between The Salvation Army's trading arm (SATCoL) and Plan B Circular operates what they say is the first commercial-scale polyester textile-to-textile recycling facility in Europe – technology adapted from a bottle recycling plant.

Project Re:Claim turns old clothes and bedding into polyester pellets (rPET) for use in new products but Tim Cross says UK law must make manufacturers more sustainable

The Salvation Army collects the items and those that cannot be reused in their current form are shredded and melted.

Impurities such as dead skin cells and hair are removed and polyester pellets (rPET) are produced which can be used to make new clothes.

"It's the future: using the clothing we have today to make the clothing that we need tomorrow," says Plan B Circular founder Tim Cross.

"We process 500kg of fabric an hour but we could easily scale up if there was demand.

"The problem is encouraging clothing manufacturers to change from using virgin polyester to recycled polyester from old textiles. And to design their new clothes to be easily recycled at their end of life."

"A polyester blazer doesn't need nylon buttons and labels. A sports top doesn't need metal zips. It can all be polyester."

That is important because the plant can only recycle items that are 100% polyester.

Majonne Frost says the Salvation Army would like to see all worn-out textiles turned back into new clothing

Most clothing "is a fibre mix like polyester-cotton, or often three or four different materials," says Majonne Frost, head of sustainability at SATCoL.

Researchers are trialling ways to separate these fibres , external , but doing it at scale remains difficult and costly, so most of those items are eventually destroyed.

Project Re:Claim says its rPET requires 89% less carbon to make than virgin polyester.

"We send the pellets back to China in what would otherwise be empty shipping containers, and it's spun back into yarn," Cross adds.

"We have the technology but we're way behind with legislation. It absolutely should be driving the way we design and make clothing."

The rPET pellets are batch tested and any that fail the quality test for new garments are reused for other products, such as car mats.

From high seas to high fashion: The students making new clothes from old sails

Designer brings items 'back to life' by repairing

EU rules are already changing , external and are forcing manufacturers to reduce the waste they produce, their environmental impact, and to make the industry circular.

It must ensure products are not only made from recycled content but are themselves recyclable at the end of their lives.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs , external (Defra) says it is "funding the UK Textiles Pact , external , which is driving ambitious targets to cut waste and increase the life cycle of materials".

In addition, Defra says "a taskforce of experts and businesses is looking at options to reduce waste in homes and businesses and will report back on next steps later this year".

Scraps of "wet blue" leather are sorted, shredded and reformed in Peterborough, "saving 18,000 tonnes from landfill" according to Gen Phoenix

The leather waste is broken down into fibres that are then re-entangled into a new fabric using water jets

Peterborough-based Gen Phoenix feels global consumer attitudes and legislation are beginning to drive change.

Every year it recycles thousands of tonnes of waste leather into new fabric which has been used by major brands, including Dr Martens, Nike and Coach.

It also specialises in train, bus and aviation seating.

"Jet2 was our first commercial customer, and now we're on one in every five commercial aircraft flying today," says chief executive John Kennedy.

"Our material has similar properties to traditional leather but with an 80% lower carbon footprint and it's lighter. Weight is important for airlines.

"We've saved more than 18,000 tonnes of material from landfill."

Paul Southall, head of sustainability for Jet2, says he is proud of its partnership with the recycling firm.

"Their innovative material is much lighter than traditional leather, which reduces fuel burn and therefore means a reduction in CO2 emissions," he says.

"It can also be recycled into new aircraft seating at the end of its life, reducing waste and giving us a responsible option for our cabin interiors."

John Kennedy says Gen Z is raising the importance of sustainability in the textile industry

Leather is itself a waste product from the food industry, but still much is wasted that Gen Phoenix feels could be salvaged.

"If you think of an animal hide, it's the bits like the neck, the shoulders, the armpits, the belly – bits that don't make good finished leather," says Richard Peace, the company's senior director of research and technology.

The company ships in the waste as "wet blue" – the name given to hides partway through the leather process – from tanneries around the world.

It breaks the leather down into a fibre fluff, which is sprayed on to thin sheets of tissue paper.

The sheets are then sandwiched around a fabric – usually recycled polyester – before high-powered water jets bind all the fibres back together.

The upcycled leather can be produced with different finishes and in different thicknesses

Called hydro-entanglement, it forms the new fabric without the need for resin binders, making the new product more easily recyclable.

"The importance of sustainability is seeing a groundswell, both in terms of legislation and consumer attitude - especially with Gen Z coming through," says Kennedy.

"Brands are definitely more invested and are being fairly quiet about the great work they're doing."

Tuze Mekik, Dr. Martens' global director of sustainability, says: "While these products currently represent a small part of our range, the growth seen in previous seasons reflects the exciting opportunities that can emerge when businesses like Dr Martens and Gen Phoenix collaborate to reimagine waste."

Gen Phoenix is continuing to innovate, developing technology to also recycle finished leather waste, but Kennedy adds: "Peterborough is where we do all of our manufacturing and R&D (research and development), and while we may establish other sites, this is where the magic happens."

Watch: What we know so far about Nvidia CEO resignation

One of the AI industry's most important figures has resigned amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive.

Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset.

Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair.

Huang admitted , external earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children.

Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters.

Nvidia stocks plummet in US after CEO Jensen Huang quits in wake of affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia's board met on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company.

It had 11 directors on its board, including Huang. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors.

But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member.

It thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions" to Nvidia, which it said were "profound".

There was no mention of the accusations of adultery.

Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO .

It is less clear is who will replace Huang on a permanent basis.

One possibility is Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky. He has been at the company as long as Huang, and for years led its product engineering work.

Huang's children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia in senior roles, but they are relatively young and inexperienced.

And there is also the option of Ian Buck, who runs high-performance computing at the firm. He developed the technology which allowed graphics cards to be used for other computing tasks, which enabled Nvidia to capitalise on the growth of AI.

A New York Times report at the weekend revealed Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who US intelligence officials believed was a spy for Beijing.

She had previously been photographed with him on several occasions.

The tech giant's board of directors launched an independent external investigation on Sunday following the reports. They earlier said Huang's interactions with the woman were "not unusual or unexpected".

Then on Wednesday, the New York Times reported Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him.

She did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - at an event

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Jensen Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the west coast of the US.

He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia.

Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic with incredibly high standards for his staff.

He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.

The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with US President Donald Trump.

At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang.

Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?

US officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external .

She was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023.

Her company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, which the firm said had been investigated and debunked.

However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singaporean government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips.

The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment.

It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing.

When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not.

China has rejected the spying allegations as "entirely groundless".

Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond

Nvidia hires major New York law firm to investigate Jensen Huang affair

Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world - so the slump in its value which followed Huang's resignation hits investors large and small.

The firm is also at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among US lawmakers.

Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the concern is if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.

The US advantage is in large part because of companies like Nvidia, working with producers such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.

Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.

This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero.

He has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.

The revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China .

Nvidia boss Jensen Huang and US President Donald Trump at the White House

After news broke out about the first affair, Nvidia launched an independent investigation and hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.

It will be led by Joon Kim, a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District who is now a litigation partner at the law firm.

US President Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating the scandal, adding that Huang told him he had been unaware the woman he was with was a spy.

Huang has also been asked to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees on 18 November, but has yet to say he will comply.

There is no clear successor for Jensen Huang at Nvidia

Founded by Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for gaming.

Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates .

Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did, effectively building the infrastructure from scratch.

He bet on AI at a time when "there were no customers for the stuff he was building", Witt told the BBC.

Every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure like Amazon, Google and Microsoft now use Nvidia chips.

Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world.

Lori Huang and her husband at a state dinner by Trump for his Chinese President Xi Jinping

Jensen Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners.

They married in 1985 and have two children, Madison and Spencer.

Earlier this week, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.

Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.

Witt told the BBC that Jensen Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him."

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family.

"But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."

The trust said the fund would seek to boost the population of bumblebees across the region

A charity wants to raise £70,000 for a project aimed at boosting wildlife populations on farmland in the Thames Valley.

The Berkshire, Buckinghamshire and Oxfordshire Wildlife Trust (BBOWT) said the money would form part of its Nature Recovery Fund and would be used to tackle falling numbers of birds, bees and butterflies.

The trust said farmland bird populations had fallen by 63% since 1970, while half of the UK's 27 bumblebee species were in decline.

It said measures to help wildlife could include using fewer chemicals in farming to create healthier soil and less polluted waterways, as well as setting aside corners of grassland for animals.

BBOWT's chief executive Estelle Bailey said: "Farmland makes up 68% of our three counties, so to truly have an impact on nature's recovery, our work must expand far beyond our precious nature reserves."

In 2023, a report produced by government agencies, environmental groups and universities found one in six species in the UK were at risk of extinction.

Bailey added: "I want future generations to experience the joy of countryside filled with life - swallows darting above fields, butterflies and bumblebees feeding on abundant wildflowers, hedgerows alive with the sound of birdsong, and to eat locally grown food that supports a healthy, resilient landscape."

MN202611_kvtpjlmm0f.t:
Watch: "It destroys people, but we all make our own choices" - Marseille drug-gang members talk to BBC

Warning: Strong language and descriptions of sexual violence

Although she had just bought hashish from a drug dealer, the woman decided to call the police.

It was because, along with the illegal drugs, she had been handed a note by the young seller during their brief meeting on a Marseille housing estate in 2022.

"We're being held captive and need help. We are 15-years-old," it read.

The teenage dealer, a French court heard earlier this year, was one of two boys being held by a gang which they had both initially approached looking for paid work - albeit illegal.

One boy had been tasked with handling money, the other worked streets around the Frais-Vallon estate. Soon though, bosses had accused them of being responsible for "shortfalls" in takings.

What followed were regular beatings, the court was told, and being forced to dance naked in front of a camera as a form of blackmail. One of the boys was also raped.

Hours after the woman was passed the note, the two teenagers had tried to escape from a second-storey window, injuring themselves in the process. One managed to get away, while the other was caught, beaten and stabbed, but survived.

Arrests were made. Photos on the phone of one of the boys' alleged torturers showed several other young men in a similarly distressed condition. Six men have since been handed hefty sentences for what happened to the two teenagers.

The boys' story highlights the grip that drug gangs hold over parts of France's second city.

While the blend of Mediterranean culture, street art and hip-hop scene has made Marseille a popular tourist destination - beyond the city centre, it is another story.

After months of trying, a BBC team managed to enter this dangerous world - centred on deprived streets and high-rise housing estates in the port city, which police do not enter lightly.

We found an environment where ruthless gangs lure vulnerable young people with promises of easy money, but end up trapping them in a world of drug dealing, brutality and exploitation.

We saw how gangs use social media to recruit hitmen and spoke to several young men caught up in the violence. From prison, one gang member accused of involvement in several murders explained how his "cold-bloodedness" had helped him rise through the ranks.

A still image from one of DZ Mafia's notorious video statements

The city's most powerful gang, DZ Mafia, emerged victorious from a bloody turf war and is now one of the most feared criminal organisations in France.

DZ is the official internet country code for Algeria, where one of the gang's founders, a French-Algerian called Mehdi Laribi, was detained earlier this year under a French arrest warrant.

The criminal outfit rose to prominence in 2023, when it became the first French gang to capitalise on its notoriety by releasing video statements - using social media to market itself as a brand - says the head of the country's anti-drug trafficking unit, Dimitri Zoulas.

Its most recent statement came in July, when the mayor of a nearby town had to be placed in police protection, after intelligence suggested he was in danger of being targeted by the group.

In an online video, six masked men dressed in black stood behind a table - as one of them read a statement denying DZ Mafia's involvement.

Inside Marseille's drug gangs - watch on YouTube now , external

France's expanding illegal drugs market - which has seen a surge in cocaine imports alongside high volumes of cannabis and synthetic drugs - has also helped the gang grow rapidly.

The number of cocaine users in France is expected soon to reach two million, says Zoulas, up from 600,000 in 2017. Drug smuggling across France generates €7bn (£5.9bn) a year, involving 200,000 people, he adds.

Many of those distributing the drugs are children and the authorities say the number of minors caught up in trafficking is increasing. During 2025, more than 10,000 children were involved in some way, according to official figures.

DZ Mafia is a prime example. To reach more customers, it needs more gang members - more children.

We have found it is now recruiting young people from across France - not just to sell drugs, but to carry out kidnap, torture and murder.

They are a generation seen as easy to corrupt, but also expendable, by the kingpins who typically control them from prison or overseas.

And, as police and judges warn, once these children enter Marseille's underworld, it is very hard to get them out.

Karine was called by a doctor about her son Hugo: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head"

Few know the human cost of Marseille's gangs like mother Karine Brouillard - who lives at the other end of France, almost as far from the Mediterranean coast as you can get.

Her son, Hugo, first ran away aged 15 - from his home in a village in the Nord department - after an argument with his family. He was picked up by police three days later, almost 1,000km (600 miles) away in Marseille, with money and cannabis on him. He was taken home.

But several years later, in 2023, Hugo planned to return south, telling his parents he had secured a holiday job at a restaurant near Marseille.

"He gave regular updates," Karine remembers. "He called me, everything was going well."

Three weeks later, a doctor called. Karine says she will never forget his words: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head."

Police believe Hugo was brought for medical help from a gang-controlled area and suspect he was involved with one.

DZ Mafia wields power in Marseille's Quartier Nord

Our best way into Quartier Nord, where DZ Mafia wields power, is with the help of resident Fadella Ouidef, a 41-year-old mother-of-four who gives us a tour.

Thirty-seven seconds after entering one housing estate, we find ourselves cornered.

Car horns sound the moment Fadella's Peugeot passes a gang checkpoint - the teenagers manning the post immediately spot our camera. "Wait, stop filming," Fadella warns, as a grey 4x4 forces us to the side of the road.

"I'm making a report for my housing association," she tells the inquisitive driver. He eventually agrees to let us leave if we stop filming.

It is unnerving to see a non-police vehicle move so assertively and a relief to watch it leave.

"Lately, the gangs have been very aggressive," explains Fadella. "What we simply try to do is make sure our young people understand what's happening is wrong."

Fadella speaks to a wider fear among local families: that their children are enticed by huge sums of money to take a criminal path that robs them of their innocence.

Camil, who claims to have left DZ Mafia, only agreed to speak to the BBC away from the city - on a boat

Money is what led one young man to spend his teenage years with DZ Mafia.

In order for our interviewees to speak freely, or because of safety concerns, we have agreed to protect their identities.

Camil tells us he worked up the gang's ranks to "running security" in one area it controls.

The now 20-year-old, who claims to have left the group, is highly suspicious of our presence, but agrees to tell us how the gang recruits young members.

"They know how to get inside your head. Whatever you want, they give to you," he says. This can range from nice cars and spacious apartments, to drugs and prostitutes, he explains.

"You feel loyalty because of what they give you. You'll stay until the very end, until either death or prison."

Camil also gives a sobering assessment of what happens if the gang identifies a weakness in a recruit: "They'll exploit it. You're their bitch, it's over."

DZ Mafia member, Adam - not his real name - tells us he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad when we speak to him in a Snapchat video call.

He is currently in prison awaiting trial, after being implicated in several murders.

"People noticed my determination, my cold-bloodedness and, without wanting to, I climbed up the ladder of the gang," says Adam. "It became my place, I had to roll with it."

During the chat, he agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".

"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."

"Thank you, see you soon" reads graffiti on a wall, alongside price lists for cocaine, hashish and marijuana

We challenge Adam on whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality.

He says he is "feeling in-part guilty" but claims to have no regrets.

"If I hadn't done all of this, there are other people who would have done that in my place, and so on. I am just another brick in the wall," he says.

Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".

At a so-called deal point in a social housing estate - sealed off and controlled by DZ Mafia - price lists for cocaine, hashish and marijuana are graffitied on a wall.

The estate acts as a natural fortress for drug dealers. With one major road in and out, they can control the flow of customers and see if the police are coming.

It is not uncommon for the sound of automatic gunfire to fill the night air in these areas.

After months of negotiations, a deal-point manager from a rival gang agrees to meet us where he works.

Gang member "Joe" says he was making €3,000 (£2,500) per month aged 13

We enter the estate early in the morning, the birdsong and children walking to school providing a stark contrast to the industrial-scale criminal operation that takes place here.

"Joe" says he was making €3,000 (£2,500) a month when he was 13. Now he says that has risen to between €5,000 and €10,000 a month.

He seems to see his life path as pre-ordained, albeit a lucrative one.

We ask Joe if he thinks about the lives lost because of the violence carried out by his gang, but the 23-year-old has also long made peace with the pain and destruction drug trafficking can cause.

"It destroys people, but we all make our own choices," he shrugs.

The work that Joe's gang and DZ Mafia are doing represents a threat to national security, says Zoulas, of the anti-drug trafficking unit.

There are road accidents, as well as family violence, depressions, suicides and more than 700 overdoses each year, he says, "and it distorts the economy".

"We are heading towards a potential systemic breakdown of the criminal justice system."

DZ Mafia members filmed firing guns from a balcony in Marseille - the footage was then posted on social media

Police have had success in Marseille and other cities against drug gangs.

Criminal operations are being frustrated, more kingpins arrested and drugs seized.

Since 2024, about 1,000 individuals associated with DZ Mafia have been arrested, and 600 incarcerated, police say.

But overall, it is a battle that is becoming more arduous, rather than easier.

As gangs seek to widen their operations, or replace members who have been arrested or killed, social media has become a potent recruitment tool - especially since the Covid pandemic, when many street-drug sales jumped online.

On social media, we found countless posts advertising jobs in Marseille for aspiring drivers, couriers and hitmen, often with glamourised AI-generated images.

Nets are also being cast wider, as it becomes harder to entice young people locally because they know more about what might happen to them.

The ads can reach teenagers in most corners of France - including Paris, Nantes and Lille - and serve as a powerful pull to Marseille, and the Quartier Nord, police say.

Online advertising has also changed the typical profile of someone who would join a gang's ranks, say law enforcement officials.

Now, it is often someone without a criminal past, but who has exploitable vulnerabilities, like having a difficult family life.

"These people are recruited by unscrupulous sponsors who send them into the lion's den," explains Thibaut Fontaine, the head of France's anti-organised-crime unit.

Their lack of criminal experience, he says, makes them easier to arrest quickly.

Karine still has no idea why her son, Hugo, was shot.

Asked what she would say to gang leaders recruiting children and young men in Marseille, she says: "They destroy families. Little sisters, little brothers, grandparents. But then, I don't think those people have a heart, really."

The restaurant where her son said he was going to work did exist, but staﬀ there told Karine they had never recruited anyone called Hugo.

The reason for his death almost certainly lies within Marseille's Quartier Nord.

Additional reporting by Marianne Baisnee, Lea Guedj and Paul Pradier

Pope Leo XIV and President Javier Milei greet each other during the pope's visit to Argentina

Pope Leo XIV has said Argentina's economy must benefit everyone including the poor, in a diplomatic but pointed critique of President Javier Milei's austerity measures.

The Pope was speaking as he arrived in Buenos Aires, the second stop on a 12-day tour of Latin America, only three weeks after having had surgery for lung cancer.

In response, right-wing leader Milei said his government was working to avoid "punishing the Argentines of tomorrow in order to benefit the Argentines of today".

This leg of the Pope's journey was expected be the most politically sensitive, with the president's agenda of slashing public spending having been denounced by the Catholic Church for hitting the poorest hardest.

"The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy," Pope Leo said.

He stressed the plight of those who, "despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household's needs", and urged that "particular concern be shown for those affected by illness, dependency and disability" - a veiled reference to the government's controversial cuts to disability assistance.

In what appeared to be a rebuke of Milei's combative style and language, the Pope said strengthening democracy required a "willingness to listen" and the "careful use of words".

Milei had been particularly outspoken about Leo's predecessor Pope Francis, whom he called "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor.

On Sunday, however, Milei struck a conciliatory tone, calling Francis an "exceptional figure" and "undoubtedly the most important Argentine in history".

He was also keen to welcome the current Pope earlier, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy".

Pope Leo urged Argentina to safeguard its democracy. "Those who exercise authority have a duty to act with prudence, to acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them, and to direct their decisions toward the good of the entire community," he said.

In his own address welcoming Leo to Argentina, Milei defended his libertarian policies, saying the rights to life, liberty and property are the backbone of Argentina's constitution and of Western democracies.

The Argentine leader, who has said he will seek re-election next year, is a strong supporter of US President Donald Trump, who has criticised Pope Leo for his opposition to the Iran war .

Pope Leo's trip to Argentina has been described as a homage to Francis, who did not return to his homeland during his own papacy.

The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".

Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.

The man identified himself as a pianist on the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship (file photo)

A cruise ship pianist was found treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast after falling overboard, according to US media reports.

Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island on Friday and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.

"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Grant Garrett was quoted as saying, recalling the moment he and Sean Norton spotted him.

The man, who has not yet been identified, was taken to hospital in a stable condition, the US Coast Guard told the BBC, adding it was investigating the incident.

The fishermen say the man identified himself as a pianist on a 14-deck cruise ship called the Ovation of the Seas.

"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.

The Coast Guard said in a statement it had received a report from "a Good Samaritan who recovered a conscious individual from the water".

The person was handed over to Newport Beach Lifeguards, who confirmed he was an employee of the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship, it said.

Lifeguard officials believe he may have fallen overboard at around 02:30, about nine hours before he was discovered.

"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS.

Norton credited the man's survival to unusually warm ocean temperatures.

"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said, which equates to about 24C.

"A different year, no way he makes it," Norton said.

The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring the Pacific, with ocean temperatures about 3.05C above average.

In a statement to the BBC, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson said: "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time.

"To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."

Lisa Nandy says she "would wager" that sexual abuse in the media industry is still happening

Abuse in the media industry is probably still happening as organisations are not doing enough to protect women, the culture secretary has warned in the wake of Russell Brand's conviction.

Lisa Nandy told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme: "Time is up, it really is time for the media industry to take this seriously."

She added that since entering government, "many people" from within the industry had reached out to her "to allege that things have happened to them".

Brand is due to be sentenced on Monday after being convicted last week of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, following allegations from multiple women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.

Nandy was asked whether she believed there was still exploitation and abuse within the media industry, following the Brand trial and cancellation of Channel 4 reality show Married at First Sight after the BBC revealed rape allegations.

She said: "I do not see that much has changed in terms of the way that institutions in the media industry and across public life, including politics, deal with women who very bravely come forward to allege abuse."

Nandy added that there was often no protection and a "very heavy cost" for women who speak up in industries such as media and politics, pointing to power imbalances and short-term contracts some staff members are given.

"Hand on heart, I can't say to you as the culture secretary that this is not happening today. In fact, if I had to wager, I would say it is," she said.

Nandy said many had come forward from within the industry, including from the BBC.

But she added that the BBC had been an "exemplar" in signing up to the industry body to protect whistleblowers - the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority - and urged other organisations to follow suit.

A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster "has made a significant commitment to improve its culture, processes and standards".

"Last year, following an independent culture review, we set out the behavioural expectations for everyone who works with or for the BBC and we were clear action would be taken if these were not met," the spokesperson added.

Brand found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault

Starting his career as a stand-up comedian, Brand became a household name as a host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth. He also had his own radio programmes on BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

During Brand's trial, he faced allegations from six women and was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault . The women revealed how Brand used his fame to force them into sexual activity.

Following his conviction, a BBC spokesperson said there could be "no place for the abuse of power", adding: "Across the industry we must work together to ensure that anyone who suffers at someone else's hand feels able to report it, that their concerns are taken seriously and that they are listened to."

The corporation restated its apology to staff who felt they could not speak up with concerns about Brand's behaviour when he worked at the BBC between 2006 and 2008, because he was seen as "too influential".

Channel 4, which aired Big Brother and its spin-off programmes at the time Brand was a presenter, said it recognised the "profound impact of these crimes".

Dormice have become much rarer in the UK as woodlands and hedgerows are lost

Dormouse numbers may be recovering in England and Wales after years of decline, offering a rare piece of good news for one of our best-loved mammals.

The animal has disappeared from much of the countryside with conservationists warning of a long-term collapse in its population.

However, new data suggests dormouse numbers increased between 2020-2025, a period that coincided with warmer springs and summers.

Scientists believe these conditions may help dormice survive, by boosting food supplies and reducing the time they spend asleep.

That gives the animals more opportunity to breed and build up fat reserves ahead of winter.

Even during spring and summer, when it's cold and wet, dormice can go into short periods of deep sleep

But conservationists caution that many questions remain unanswered, and say protecting the woodlands and hedgerows where dormice live remains essential to their long-term survival.

The only native species of dormice in the UK is the hazel dormouse. Once widespread across the country, they are now largely confined to southern England and parts of Wales. They have become much rarer as large areas of woodland are lost and so far native populations have disappeared from around 20 English counties.

The National Dormouse Monitoring Programme, led by the conservation charity People's Trust for Endangered Species (PTES), has been monitoring sites in England and Wales since 1998.

It found that since 2000, dormouse numbers have fallen by almost 60%, equivalent to an average annual decline of 3.5%.

More recently, however, there are signs that trend may be reversing. The data suggests the population increased by almost 10% between 2020 and 2025, although researchers stress there is considerable uncertainty around that estimate.

The apparent improvement coincides with a period of warmer, drier-than-average springs and summers.

Report co-author Ian White of PTES described the "upturn" as "welcome good news" which gives grounds for "cautious optimism".

But he added: "We mustn't lose sight of the bigger picture: populations remain almost 60% lower than they were in 2000."

The hazel dormouse spends most of its time in trees, coming out at night to eat flowers, insects, berries and nuts

The hazel dormouse is famous for spending much of the year asleep. It hibernates from around October to May, spending the winter in a nest on the ground.

Even during spring and summer, dormice can go into short periods of deep sleep, known as torpor, when the weather is cold and wet, or food is scarce. This helps the small rodent conserve energy.

Researchers believe warmer summers may be reducing the need for torpor, leaving dormice with more energy for feeding and breeding.

They say more research is needed to understand what longer-term impacts climate change could have on the species.

Dr Charlotte Armitage, an ecologist who worked on the survey, said significant uncertainties remain, including how dormice will respond to warmer, wetter winters.

However, she said warmer summer conditions are likely to give the animals more energy to reproduce and raise additional litters.

"This is good news, but we can't be complacent," she told BBC News.

"We still need to protect their habitat, do more research into the effects of climate change and carry out effective woodland management for the benefit of dormice."

Despite only being on their second date, this couple had already discussed love languages

I'm "words of affirmation", and so is my husband. This is supposedly our shared love language.

But, while we do like receiving compliments, they make us both feel a bit awkward.

Despite this, our result was confidently defined when we took the original Love Languages Quiz online, a personality test published by US pastor Gary Chapman who first came up with the five types of expressing and receiving love in 1992.

I'm sceptical. Does the theory really know more about us than our own lived experience of a 10-year marriage?

The five love languages are: Quality Time, Acts of Service, Words of Affirmation, Receiving Gifts, and Physical Touch - and they feel more ubiquitous than ever.

Contestants on dating shows ask each other their love languages; "My love language is…" is a common prompt on dating apps.

According to the Love Languages website, my husband and I are just two out of more than 150 million people to have taken this particular quiz.

Even though we scored much lower on some of the other languages, they speak more directly to us.

For example I love spending "quality time" with my husband, and feel much more loved by him making lists of films to watch with me than when he pays me a compliment.

But where did the idea of these five neat categories come from? And are they relevant for modern dating and relationships?

How do you show your partner you love them?

Unlike other relationship theories - such as attachment theory - the concept of love languages doesn't have scientific origins.

Chapman said the theory came to him after observing couples during counselling sessions he held in his parish.

Counselling psychologist Dr Sarah Emmerson told the BBC that love languages are still mentioned regularly in her sessions.

"There's almost no-one out there who hasn't taken that quiz," she said. "[Couples] quite frequently bring that in and say, 'So my partner is Physical Touch and I'm Acts of Service, so this doesn't work'.

"Research has proven that there isn't a lot of validity to the idea that there are only five ways in which people show love, and that everybody fits neatly into these categories. But people still gravitate towards it, and we have to wonder why that might be."

Fan edits have tried to guess the love languages of Nick and Charlie in Heartstopper

For some, talking about love languages can simply be a useful introduction to thinking about how they communicate their needs to their partner.

Psychotherapist Georgina Sturmer said that it helps people think about "what you really like in a relationship, and what do other people really like" but points out it's "hugely limited" and risks "oversimplifying everything".

In recent years, many therapists have also warned that Chapman's examples refer too readily to scripture and unequal relationship dynamics.

In the Love Languages book Chapman describes counselling a woman, Ann, whose husband of 10 years is hostile and verbally abusive towards her, including frequently telling her he hates her.

His love language, Ann tells Chapman, is specifically sexual physical touch.

When Ann says she finds it "hard to be sexually responsive" to him, Chapman advises her that she should "rely heavily upon [her] faith in God" to make herself have sex with her husband more often.

This example also exposes another problem - that love languages can be used to coerce partners into showing or receiving love in a way they're not comfortable with.

"There's a risk if someone says, 'well my love language is receiving gifts, so you must give me gifts all the time, or my love language is physical touch, so you must be physically intimate with me all the time," Sturmer said.

The BBC has contacted the Love Languages team for comment.

Chapman's theory of love languages is 35 years old but is often still mentioned by couples

So what can couples do if they want to understand each other, and themselves, better?

Listen to your partner: "Don't just wait until you can speak, but try to hear what they are saying and acknowledge their feelings," Dr Emmerson said.

Remember that disagreements are normal: "Healthy relationships often feature debate and disagreement," Sturmer said. "The challenge is not about avoiding rupture, it's about finding ways to repair it that can leave the relationship feeling stronger."

But, Dr Emmerson added, you should "pick the right time to talk about things that are difficult - not late at night, not when they've just come through the door".

Respond to bids for connection: Dr Emmerson said you should "try to be emotionally responsive to your partner when they are seeking connection" - even if they're doing so in subtle ways.

"This could be asking for a hug, or just telling you about something they just saw on their phone."

How soon is too soon when it comes to thinking about Christmas and your finances?

The answer, of course, is that it is never too soon. Save early and the cost becomes more manageable.

The squeeze is harder for some than others, with charity Barnardo's warning that some parents will skip meals so their kids get a Christmas dinner with the trimmings.

But, debt advice charity StepChange is offering tips to everyone, to avoid Christmas spending leading to a financially painful new year.

The best way to avoid a difficult January, it says, is to make a realistic plan before the spending begins.

Small decisions now can make a big difference later. Its tips include:

Budget for Christmas in full . So, that's not just presents, a budget should include the cost of food and drink, travel, parties, presents, postage, decorations and other festive extras

Spread the cost . Don't just rely on your December paypacket. Also, make a shopping list before Black Friday on 27 November - it is only a discount if you were going to buy it anyway

Book your train journey now . Advance tickets, if available, are cheaper

Set spending limits . Put a cap on the bill for Christmas socialising, and have a quiet conversation with family and friends about how much to spend on presents

Stocktake before the big food shop . Check your cupboards, fridge and freezer before you go shopping and plan meals around food you already have. Make a list of what you need and compare prices.

Think twice . Can you afford what you are going to buy? Can you afford the repayments if it's bought on credit? And, do you really need it?

"Christmas is a time when we want to enjoy ourselves and make things special for the people we care most about," said Vikki Brownridge, chief executive of StepChange.

"But it can also put a lot of pressure on household budgets, and it is key to take steps to get ahead of any January financial blues."

If you are concerned about Christmas leaving you in debt, then it is best to seek advice well before things become unmanageable.

The independent MoneyHelper website has a guide to finding free debt advice near you , external .

There are also tools to work out if you are receiving all the benefits and grants you are entitled to, and tips on how to draw up a budget.

And it is really important to watch out for scams at this time of year. Fraudsters will take any opportunity to catch you out, especially when you are under pressure financially.

Dr Frances O'Hagan is an Armagh-based GP, in addition to her role in the BMA

A new contract with GPs, accompanied by an extra £40m investment, will make it "easier" to get a doctor's appointment, Northern Ireland's health minister has said.

Robbie Butler has secured an agreement with GPs more than a year after family doctors withdrew some services in protest over a lack of adequate funding.

Dr Frances O'Hagan from the British Medical Association (BMA) said the £40m would be used to hire more GPs and receptionists to increase capacity in surgeries.

However, she said the investment was only "a start" and was "by no means all that we need" in order to address all of the demands that GPs are facing.

The total in-year value for the 2026/27 General Medical Services Contract is worth approximately £17m.

The Department of Health (DoH) said it had committed the extra £40m over two years for "measurable improvements in patient access and primary care activity".

O'Hagan argued the "money that's spent in Northern Ireland in primary care is woeful compared to what it is anywhere else in the four nations".

"We are currently spending less than 5% of the [health] budget in primary care, for us to provide 95% of the consultations," she told the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme.

"It is well recognised that a working budget - that is good for patients - is around 10%, so we're about half of what we should be."

O'Hagan, who chairs the BMA's Northern Ireland general practitioners committee (NIGPC), suggested it was a small sum compared to the size of the population.

"If you're looking at £20m per year... I mean, we've two million patients," she said.

"That's £10 per patient, per year. In reality what is that going to provide you?"

The Department of Health says it will give an additional £20m a year for two years for "improvements in patient access and primary care activity"

Butler, who was appointed in August, told the same programme that securing a new GP contract after the long-running dispute was a "first-day priority of mine".

"This year the deal is worth about £17.7m and that's been part of an ongoing negotiation with the GP federations and we've secured that and I think we're in a good place," he said.

Butler was asked where he had found the extra investment money at a time when Stormont had failed to agree a budget, and if such funding could be guaranteed.

"The additional £40m will come over this next two years and that will be subject to provisions within that [GP contract] deal, particularly towards the engagement in the neighbourhood model," Butler said.

The health minister said the investment package "must deliver more appointments and services"

The neighbourhood model is the term used to describe the expansion of GP surgery services to include "multi-disciplinary teams" working from one site.

That means that other healthcare staff such as physiotherapists, mental healthcare workers and social workers hold clinics alongside GPs.

The minister said the multi-disciplinary provision was the "direction of travel for the wider health and social care sector".

He agreed the £40m investment he had negotiated was "not a panacea" in terms of solving all the problems that patients face when trying to get GP appointments.

"But we do know that with the money that's being invested in digital IT, that a lot of the solutions that will come forward will be achieved through modernisation of our systems," he said.

Butler added: "There are some general practices which don't seem to be having the same issues with patient access, so we need to see where the good practice is and then try to extend this right across the province."

A GP contract is a formal agreement between GP partners or practices and the DoH to provide general medical services.

In May 2025, Butler's predecessor Mike Nesbitt imposed a disputed financial package on Northern Ireland GPs after they rejected the deal.

The move had triggered a work to rule , which included doctors ignoring non-essential paperwork, limiting appointments to the BMA's recommended safe limit of 25 per day and the withdrawal of non-contractual services.

The chair of Stormont's Health Committee gave a cautious welcome to the ending of the dispute between GPs and the DOH and the extra funding for GP services.

"It is welcome investment - it should improve care, it should improve access and it should improve patient outcomes," Philip McGuigan told Good Morning Ulster.

However, he said the committee would want to see more details, including where the money was coming from.

"I'm a wee bit cautious because we have the minister saying there's finality here and we have the BMA saying: 'This is an improvement but we need to continue negotiations.'

"So I think patients – your listeners - will rightly judge this agreement on whether they can actually get an appointment when they need one. "

McGuigan added: "We want to see just exactly where the minister has found the money and the impact that might have on the wider healthcare system."

BBC News NI health correspondent Marie-Louise Connolly

Northern Ireland needs more GPs to deliver much needed appointments for the public.

Acquiring more GPs needs considerable long-term investment and what the department has announced appears to fall short of what general practice has said is required.

Recently, GPs told the Health Committee that general practice in Northern Ireland received less than 6% of the entire health budget.

Dr O'Hagan said that wasn't nearly enough to fund the number of doctors required in each practice to meet growing demand.

While she said 10% of the health budget was the minimum they could accept - 15% was a longer term ambition.

Those figures translate closer to £80m per year as opposed to the £20m allocated by the health minister,

Clearly what is good about the funding announcement is that it ends a 12-month dispute between the department and GPs.

At least, if required, new negotiations can begin again.
